https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Michigan High School Athletic Association Representative Council meeting held in East Lansing on May 3, 2021, distributed to member districts with the instruction that changes take effect Aug. 1, 2021 unless otherwise indicated. The Council adopted rule changes across regulations, officiating, and individual sports, including a move of all fall high school practice starts to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021, permanent authorization of multi-school district cooperative programs in nine sports, adoption of girls wrestling as an individual division, and a CPR certification attestation for head coaches. It also approved the 2021-22 budget, which forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
MHSAA Representative Council, East Lansing, May 3, 2021. Mark Uyl served as recorder. Eighteen Council members were present (including Eric Albright of Midland, Nicole Carter of Novi, Karen Leinaar of Bear Lake, Vic Michaels of Detroit, and Alex Tiseo of Marquette); Jay Alexander of Detroit was absent. Scott Eldridge and Bill Zaagman of Lansing also attended. Minutes of the March 26, 2021 Council meeting and the March 25 and April 21, 2021 Executive Committee meetings were approved on a motion by Kris Isom, supported by Chris Miller.

**Administration report**

| Measure | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| High school members, 2020-21 (as of April 1, 2021) | 747 |
| Junior high/middle school members (as of April 1, 2021) | 751 |
| Comparable figures as of April 1, 2019 | 753 and 819 |
| Elementary schools with 6th-grade participation | 69 |
| High school cooperative agreements / teams (as of April 4, 2019) | 355 / 640 |
| Junior high-middle school cooperative agreements / teams | 86 / 330 |
| Eligibility advancement applications, 2020-21 | 0 (lowest since 1987-88; high was 94 in 1991-92) |
| Educational Transfer Forms, 2020-21 through April 5, 2021 | 110 (213 in 2019-20; 266 in 2015-16) |
| Out-of-State Practice travel forms, 2020-21 | 6 (72 prior year) |
| Athletic Director In-Service/Update registrants | more than 732 |
| Coaches Advancement Program participants, 2021-22 | more than 2,000, with over 1,200 in CAP 1 |

Public-to-public transfers were the most common category (67) and the divorce exception (#8) the most frequent reason (40). More than 33,000 CAP levels will have been completed since the start of 2004-05. Officials' registrations continued a decade-long decline.

**Ongoing business**
A task force was formed to meet three times over spring and summer on out-of-season contact days. The waiver of the previous academic record regulation (Regulation I, Section 7) was extended for fall 2021 sports. All fall high school practices move to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021, and thereafter to the 16th Monday before Thanksgiving. Multi-school district cooperative programs in baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis, and wrestling were made permanent notwithstanding the 3,500-student enrollment maximum.

**Regulations**
The Council voted not to print the 2021-22 Handbook, providing a password-protected online version instead. It amended Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24 on 8th/9th grade classwork; Regulation I, Section 12(C) on all-star events, requiring written notice at least 30 calendar days prior; and Regulation II, Section 3(B) requiring CPR certification attestation for head coaches, with the non-varsity requirement effective Aug. 1, 2022.

**Sports and officials actions**
Adopted: Phantom bowling oil pattern; competitive cheer choreography study and two technical changes; sideline officials switching sides at halftime; iWanamaker golf scoring; a black quarter-zip option for gymnastics officials; a softball suspended-game policy mirroring baseball's 2020 policy; a 117-game daily tennis limit and revised seed-withdrawal handling; girls wrestling as an individual division (D1, D2, D3, D4, Girls); and a late arrival skin check. Not approved: expansion of the football 5-quarter rule, playoff region seeding by playoff points, and a tennis opt-up letter requirement. The officials rating system replaces the 1-5 scale with four categories, and baseball Quarterfinal assignments move to four umpires, increasing umpires selected at that level by 16.

**Budget and future meetings**
Two budget deficits in excess of $670,000 occurred in two of the past four years. The 2021-22 budget forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301 and a profit of $318,301 after repayment of the line-of-credit loan; salaries remain frozen. Next meetings: Dec. 3, 2021; Friday, March 25, 2022; and May 1-2, 2022, the latter to be held at Treetops Resort in Gaylord.

Accounts of Meetings. Motion by Kris Isom, supported by Chris Miller, to approve the minutes of the Representative Council meeting of March 26, 2021, and the Executive Committee meeting minutes of March 25 and April 21, 2021. Adopted.

Administration report. MHSAA membership during 2020-21 was 747 high schools and 751 junior high/middle schools as of April 1, 2021, compared with 753 and 819 respectively as of April 1, 2019. There were also 69 elementary schools with 6th-grader participation. As of April 4, 2019 there were 355 cooperative program agreements for high schools covering 640 teams, an increase of 16 programs and 33 teams over the previous year, and 86 cooperative program agreements covering 330 teams for junior high/middle schools, an increase of 1 program and 5 teams. The most frequent high school cooperative sports, in order, are ice hockey, boys and girls swimming and diving, girls softball, and boys lacrosse; at the junior high/middle school level they are boys and girls track and field, boys and girls cross country, and wrestling. No eligibility advancement applications were received during 2020-21, the lowest number since the provision began in 1987-88, compared with 3 during 2019-20, 3 during 2018-19, 6 during 2017-18, 5 during 2016-17, 5 during 2015-16, 4 during 2014-15, 14 during 2013-14, 15 during 2012-13, 9 during 2011-12, 15 during 2010-11, 2009-10 and 2008-09, and 7 during 2007-08; the highest was 94 during 1991-92. There were 110 Educational Transfer Forms processed for 2020-21 through April 5, 2021, a figure the report says cannot be compared to prior years because of the pandemic and because all spring sports transfers were eligible in 2020-21; prior-year counts were 213 for 2019-20, 215 for 2018-19, 219 for 2017-18, 237 for 2016-17, and 266 for 2015-16. Public-to-public school transfers remain the most common at 67, and the divorce exception (#8) remains the most frequent reason at 40. Six Travel Forms for Out-of-State Practice were filed during 2020-21 compared to 72 the year before; the highest number filed was 113 during 2007-08 and the lowest 40 during 2003-04, with the requirement beginning in 1994-95. A listing of violations by schools and officials between April 9, 2020 and April 8, 2021 showed a total much lower than previous years because of cancelled contests and seasons. Virtual Athletic Director In-Service and Update Meeting programs attracted more than 732 registrants in 2020-21; for the 11th year, two in-service programs for athletic department administrative assistants are planned for September. The Coaches Advancement Program has already involved more than 2,000 participants in 2021-22 with over 1,200 registrations in CAP 1, and by the end of the year individuals will have completed more than 33,000 CAP levels since the start of 2004-05. The decade-long decline in officials' registrations continued through 2020-21, with the pandemic complicating recruiting and retention. Officials Reports for spring 2020, fall 2020, and winter 2020-21 were provided, broken down by sport and by level (varsity, junior varsity, and sometimes 9th, 8th, and 7th grade); sportsmanship problems were described as statistically rare. From the National Federation of State High School Associations, the Reaching Higher event in girls volleyball will not be held in summer 2021, with final decisions on basketball summer plans due by May 15.

Legislation and litigation. Bill Zaagman reported that the State Legislature's current focus is the budget process and that he will continue monitoring bills affecting the association. Scott Eldridge reported the MHSAA is not involved in public, legislative, or judicial challenges, and provided an update on recent COVID-19 legal activity involving MDHHS and local health departments.

Ongoing business. On the COVID-19 update, the Council discussed the financial impact of the pandemic and the formation of a task force to meet three times during spring and summer to discuss out-of-season contact days and develop concrete proposals for school discussion and input during fall 2021. Staff will send a summer guidance document reminding schools that the traditional summer dead period regulation remains in place. Motion by Vic Michaels, supported by John Thompson, to extend the waiver of the previous academic record regulation (Regulation I, Section 7) for sports played in fall 2021. Adopted. On the common fall practice date, motion by Chris Miller, supported by Eric Albright, to move the start of all fall high school sports practices to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021; beginning in fall 2021 all high school fall sports may begin practice on the 16th Monday before Thanksgiving, the same as football. Adopted. Staff provided a volleyball scheduling update on input from administrators and coaches regarding the MHSAA Finals and the length of the season, noting the issue also involves the start date of winter sports. On multi-school district cooperative programs, the Council recalled that in May 2016 it approved a two-year experiment, extended for two additional school years through 2020-21, allowing two or more schools of the same public school district with the same governing board to apply for cooperative programs in nine sports regardless of the 3,500-student enrollment maximum: baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis, and wrestling, subject to a demonstrated history of inadequate participant numbers and not approvable on financial grounds. Motion by Vic Michaels, supported by Karen Leinaar, to approve these programs on a permanent basis with the same requirements as all other programs, including the two-year renewal process with league approval. Adopted. Fall Tour planning anticipates a normal Update tour with remote alternatives, covering lessons of the pandemic in remote learning and instruction, potential use of school transportation in the summer, classification and cooperative program limits, out-of-season regulations, basketball contest limitations, and the length of the girls volleyball and basketball seasons.

Regulations. Regulations I through V of the MHSAA Handbook and their interpretations were submitted for review. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Jason Mensing, to not print the MHSAA Handbook for the 2021-22 school year only and to provide an online password-protected version for administrators, with a printed and emailed supplement of changes and calendars for 2021-22 and beyond also placed online and provided to schools. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Steve Newkirk, to approve the consent package of miscellaneous changes for organization, clarity, or updating and to incorporate previously adopted changes or interpretations. Adopted. Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24: motion by John Thompson, supported by Jason Mensing, addressing students whose classwork is divided between the 8th and 9th grades, who are considered enrolled in the grade where they take the major part of their work in that term, with ties resolved to the 8th grade; a student who has completed the 7th grade at any school may be considered an 8th grader if the student does not exceed the enrollment threshold of Interpretation 46, namely enrollment in 3 high school classes of 4 taken in the 8th grade, 4 or 5 of 6, 5 of 7, or 6 of 8; this 66% allowance applies only to a student enrolled for the first time in the 8th grade and not to a student repeating the 8th grade, and a student not in the 9th grade or higher is ineligible for senior high athletics except as provided in Regulation I, Section 1(D) and Regulation III, Section 2(B). Adopted. Regulation I, Section 12(C): motion by Chris Riker, supported by Chris Miller, allowing a student who has completed a 12th-grade season in a sport to participate without loss of eligibility for other sports in one high school all-star event in that sport held after the MHSAA Final, provided the student is eligible under all MHSAA regulations including academic eligibility and amateur status, the event requires or receives no financial support from an MHSAA member school or school-related organization, and participation is approved by the principal or athletic director with written notice to the MHSAA at least 30 calendar days prior to the event. Adopted. Regulation II, Section 3(B): motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, requiring high schools to attest by each season's established deadline that all head coaches of each high school team (varsity, JV, or 9th grade) hold valid current CPR certification, with the requirement for non-varsity head coaches taking effect Aug. 1, 2022; the deadline is the latest date set for completion of the MHSAA rules meeting for the sport, a person who is head coach for more than one sport must meet the deadline for the first, and schools are expected to impose the penalty of Section 8(B) on varsity head coaches who do not comply, extended effective Aug. 1, 2022 to JV and 9th-grade coaches. Adopted. The Council also discussed extending the requirement to middle schools and was updated on a fall discussion item allowing school transportation for out-of-season summer activities.

Classification, athletic equity, and officials. The Summary of MHSAA Tournament Classification for 2021-22 was provided, with future committee topics to include a possible fifth division in sports where 600 or more schools sponsor the sport. Motion by Chris Miller, supported by Chris Riker, to approve the Athletic Equity Committee recommendation to publish a statement encouraging local review of nicknames and logos considered offensive or hurtful to minority groups, stating that the MHSAA recognizes the importance of equity in high school sports, that schools and mascots are rich in tradition and unique to each community, and that the MHSAA encourages member schools and communities to evaluate and reconsider names and mascots that may be offensive. Adopted; schools will be encouraged to review the information at fall Update and Athletic Director In-Service sessions, and the Council discussed a possible sanction of barring such schools from hosting tournaments. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Jason Mensing, to adjust the officials rating system for 2021-22 to encourage more ratings from schools with a simpler format, eliminating the 1-5 rating in favor of four categories: judgement, presence and demeanor, attitude and effort, and administration and communication. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Chris Miller, to change baseball umpire assignments at the Quarterfinal round from three umpires officiating three games with two umpires each to four umpires officiating the two Regional Final games with two umpires and the Quarterfinal game with all four, increasing the number of umpires selected at this level by 16 and matching softball practice. Adopted.

Sports Medicine and committees. The Sports Medicine Advisory Committee reported ongoing discussion of providing the Pre-participation Physical Exam on a two-year cycle with an interim Health Questionnaire in intervening years, noting that health history is the most important part of the exam and that the Health Questionnaire was established with good results in 2020-21. Council members were supplied with committee descriptions, appointment procedures, candidate lists, and a list of schools unrepresented for five years, and were encouraged to nominate superintendents, principals, small schools, females, minorities, and unrepresented schools. Committee members for 2021-22 will be published in benchmarks, and staff suggested all committee meetings remain virtual for 2021-22.

Sports activities. Bowling: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Don Gustafson, to adopt the Phantom oil pattern for the 2021-22 bowling season. Adopted. Girls competitive cheer: motion by Kris Isom, supported by Vic Michaels, to continue studying a new choreography chart awarding points based on team tumble, OLEs, vertical twist/360s, and release skills. Adopted. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Nicole Carter, to allow a connected tumbling skill to count as a new variety point for Round 3 and to allow four difficulty points for a one-leg flair at the elevator level for middle schools. Adopted. Football: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Eric Albright, to not approve expanding the 5-quarter rule to exempt special teams play. Adopted (no change). Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Kris Isom, requiring sideline officials (linesman and line judge) to change sidelines at halftime for all varsity contests, optional at subvarsity. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Chris Miller, to not approve seeding Playoff Regions based on playoff points. Adopted (no change). Golf: motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, requiring use of the iWanamaker scoring program and app during the regular season beginning in 2021-22. Adopted. Girls gymnastics: motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, adding an option for officials to wear a specified black quarter-zip with the MHSAA logo. Adopted. Boys lacrosse: a committee recommendation on voluntary coach/player contact days was referred to the task force created under the COVID-19 update for review prior to August 2021. Softball: motion by Don Gustafson, supported by John Thompson, adding a suspended game policy under which a game is suspended if called before reaching regulation or if called with the score tied, mirroring the baseball policy approved in 2020. Adopted. Tennis: motion by Vic Michaels, supported by Kris Isom, limiting a player to no more than 117 games in a given day. Adopted. Motion by Chris Riker, supported by Don Gustafson, on adjusting seeds when a seeded player withdraws on the day of the tournament. Adopted. Motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, to not approve requiring a letter when a school opts up in tennis. Adopted (no change). Wrestling: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, adding girls wrestling as an individual division rather than a new sport (D1, D2, D3, D4, Girls) using a sectionals concept with a qualifying event before the Finals, with girls still allowed to wrestle on boys teams during the team postseason. Adopted. Motion by John Thompson, supported by Don Gustafson, approving a late arrival skin check for multiple dual meets in the regular season. Adopted.

Operations. Motion by Chris Miller, supported by Jason Mensing, to approve the Quick Reference Calendars for 2021-22 and 2022-23 and the seven-year calendar of MHSAA events. Adopted. Council members were invited to vote for up to two Allen W. Bush Award candidates from the five presented, with winners notified in May, honored during fall 2021 or early 2022, and featured in the fall issue of benchmarks. The next Representative Council meeting is Dec. 3, 2021 at the MHSAA office in East Lansing; the March meeting will be the morning of Friday, March 25, 2022 in East Lansing; and the May meeting will be Sunday and Monday, May 1 and 2, 2022. Motion by Sean Jacques, supported by Karen Leinaar, to hold the May 2022 meeting at Treetops Resort in Gaylord. Adopted.

Budget. The report states that since COVID hit in March 2020 the association has managed unprecedented times with severe reductions in tournament revenue, aided by the sacrifices of member schools and tournament hosts in 2020-21. While two installments of the federal Payroll Protection program have been helpful, the reality of two budget deficits in excess of $670,000 in two of the past four years still exists. The 2021-22 budget proposes a modest increase in most ticket prices beyond the entry level of the tournament, allowing prompt repayment of a line-of-credit loan and rebuilding of reserves. The MHSAA anticipates a break-even 2020-21 fiscal year with an average spring tournament season. Staff salaries will remain frozen for 2021-22, including the hiring of three new staff members following the retirements of Nate Hampton and Peggy Montpas and the departure of Faye Verellen. The 2021-22 budget forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301 and a profit of $318,301 after repayment of the line-of-credit loan from last spring and fall. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, to approve the 2021-22 budget. Adopted.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Summary of the Michigan High School Athletic Association's Athletes and Officials Accident Medical and Concussion Care insurance programs distributed to high schools and junior high/middle schools for 2020-21. The accident medical policy, provided at no cost since the 1970-71 school year, pays up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses per claim after a $25,000 deductible in paid medical expenses has been met. A separate concussion care program in place since 2015-16 carries a policy limit of $25,000 for each accident and reimburses deductibles and co-pays left unpaid by other coverage.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Program overview**
Since the 1970-71 school year the MHSAA has provided participants at each member school and all registered officials with insurance intended to help pay excess accident medical bills for injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium; coverage is provided at no cost to eligible athletes of member schools and to registered officials. The document states it is not intended to be a complete description of coverage and exclusions.

**Who and what is covered**
Coverage applies to grades 6-12 for students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction, namely baseball, basketball (boys and girls), bowling (boys and girls), cross country (boys and girls), football, golf (boys and girls), gymnastics (girls), competitive cheer (girls), ice hockey, lacrosse (boys and girls), soccer (boys and girls), softball (girls), alpine skiing (boys and girls), swimming and diving (boys and girls), tennis (boys and girls), track and field (boys and girls), volleyball (girls), and wrestling. Students are covered in sports ending with an MHSAA tournament provided their principal attests in writing and the MHSAA agrees they were eligible under all MHSAA regulations at the time of injury. Coverage extends to travel directly to and from a scheduled event in school-sponsored transportation and to in-season participation in an allowed activity under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or designated coach.

**Exclusions and edge cases**
Student-athletes ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered. Students ineligible under local school rules but eligible under MHSAA rules are covered if allowed to practice with the team, as are students suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3 who continue practicing. Officials must be on the premises of the contest worked. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling in school-sponsored transportation and while cheering under supervision of a designated school employee, provided their activity does not exceed the safety norms of MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer. The insurance does not cover any out-of-season activities or activities occurring beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193, even if not expressly prohibited.

**Accident medical benefits**

| Benefit | Amount / condition |
| --- | --- |
| Medical expense limit | up to $1,000,000 per claim |
| Deductible | $25,000 in paid medical expenses per claim |
| Paralysis or coma cash benefit | up to $50,000, if occurring within 180 days after the accident |
| Certification waiting period | physician certifies permanence after a 16-month waiting period |
| First medical expense | must be incurred within 90 days after the accident |
| Accidental death or dismemberment | $10,000 if the event occurs within 365 days |

The MHSAA-arranged program pays medical expenses above the $25,000 deductible left unpaid by parents' or officials' insurance or other sources such as school-purchased insurance.

**Concussion care insurance**
Provided since the 2015-16 school year to athletic participants at each MHSAA member junior high/middle school and high school, paying accident medical expense benefits resulting from concussion sustained while participating in an MHSAA in-season covered activity (in-season practice or competition). Policy limit is $25,000 for each accident, with covered students, sports, and situations following the accident medical insurance. The program is intended to assure that all eligible student-athletes in grades 6 through 12, male and female, in all levels of all sports under MHSAA jurisdiction receive prompt professional attention for head injury events even if uninsured or under-insured.

**Claims administrators**
Accident medical: Mr. Bryan Cronen, FIRST AGENCY, INC., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501, phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055, bcronen@1stagency.com. Concussion care: Ms. Terri Bruner, K & K Insurance Group, 1712 Magnavox Way, Fort Wayne, IN 46801, phone 800-237-2917, fax 312-381-9077, Terri.Bruner@kandkinsurance.com. Districts are advised to make sure all high schools and junior high/middle schools are designated by their board of education as MHSAA member schools so athletes at both levels are covered by the MHSAA-purchased plan.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Informational summary titled "Athletes and Officials Accident Medical & Concussion Insurance," issued by the Michigan High School Athletic Association to high schools and junior high/middle schools for the 2020-21 school year. The document carries the caveat that it is not intended to be a complete description of coverage and exclusions.

History and purpose. Since the 1970-71 school year the MHSAA has provided participants at each member school and all registered officials with insurance intended to help pay excess accident medical bills to administer to injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium for this layer of accident medical coverage, and the coverage is provided at no cost to the eligible athletes of MHSAA member schools and to registered officials.

Scope of covered activity. Coverage is provided for grades 6-12 for all students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The enumerated sports are baseball; basketball (boys and girls); bowling (boys and girls); cross country (boys and girls); football; golf (boys and girls); gymnastics (girls); competitive cheer (girls); ice hockey; lacrosse (boys and girls); soccer (boys and girls); softball (girls); alpine skiing (boys and girls); swimming and diving (boys and girls); tennis (boys and girls); track and field (boys and girls); volleyball (girls); and wrestling.

Eligibility conditions. All eligible students who participate in interscholastic athletic activities at an MHSAA member school in sports which end with an MHSAA tournament are covered provided their school principal attests in writing and the MHSAA agrees that they were eligible under all MHSAA regulations at the time of the injury. Eligible student athletes are covered while traveling directly to and from a scheduled event as a representative of the school in transportation sponsored by the school, and while participating in season in an allowed activity under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or a coach designated by the school acting within the scope of his or her coaching duties, in those sports for which the MHSAA provides a tournament series.

Ineligibility and special cases. Student-athletes ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered. Students who are ineligible under local school rules but would be eligible under MHSAA rules are covered if they were allowed to practice with their school team. Students who are otherwise eligible but suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3 (contest disqualifications) are covered if they continue practicing with the school team. Officials must be on the premises of the contest worked to be covered under the policy. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling directly to and from interscholastic athletic events as a representative of the school in school-sponsored transportation, and while cheering at interscholastic athletic events under the direct supervision of a school employee designated by the school; to be covered by MHSAA-purchased insurance, the activity of sideline cheerleaders at interscholastic athletic events must not exceed the safety norms of MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer, meaning the height of mounts, flips, stunts, and similar elements. The document states in emphasized text that MHSAA Accident Medical Insurance does not cover any out-of-season activities or any activities occurring beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193, even if those activities are not expressly prohibited by the MHSAA.

Accident medical benefit structure. The policy will pay up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses after a deductible of $25,000 in paid medical expenses per claim has been met. The MHSAA-arranged program then pays medical expenses above the $25,000 deductible left unpaid by the parents' or official's insurance or any other sources such as school-purchased insurance. A cash benefit payment of up to $50,000 will be made if a covered person is paralyzed or in a coma within 180 days after the accident; payment will not be made until a physician certifies that, after a 16-month waiting period, the injury is permanent and irreversible, and this payment must result in disability and is in addition to payments already covered for medical expenses. The first medical expense must be incurred within 90 days after the date of the accident. An accidental death or dismemberment benefit of $10,000 is paid if either event occurs within 365 days of the date.

Accident medical claims administration. The claims administrator is Mr. Bryan Cronen, FIRST AGENCY, INC., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501, phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055, email bcronen@1stagency.com.

District action item. The document instructs in emphasized text that districts make sure all high schools and junior high/middle schools in the district are designated by their board of education as MHSAA member schools so athletes on both levels are covered by the MHSAA-purchased plan.

Concussion care insurance. Since the 2015-16 school year the MHSAA has provided athletic participants at each MHSAA member junior high/middle school and high school with insurance intended to pay accident medical expense benefits resulting from concussion. The suspected concussion must be sustained while the athlete is participating in an MHSAA in-season covered activity, defined as in-season practice or competition. The policy limit is $25,000 for each accident. Covered students, sports, and situations follow those of the accident medical insurance described above. The program intends to assure that all eligible student-athletes in MHSAA member schools in grades 6 through 12, male and female, in all levels of all sports under MHSAA jurisdiction receive prompt and professional attention for head injury events even if the child is uninsured or under-insured, and accident medical deductibles and co-pays left unpaid by other policies are reimbursed under this program.

Concussion claims administration. The claims administrator is Ms. Terri Bruner, K & K Insurance Group, 1712 Magnavox Way, Fort Wayne, IN 46801, phone 800-237-2917, fax 312-381-9077, email Terri.Bruner@kandkinsurance.com.

The district served 12,723 students in 20 schools and closed the year with a governmental-activities net position deficit of $(201,057,958), reflecting a net pension liability of $308,094,061 and a net OPEB liability of $48,088,931 under MPSERS. The most consequential operating result was in the General Fund, where fund balance increased $6.7 million to $32,734,102, a sixth consecutive year of growth, leaving the available (unassigned) balance at 19.88 percent of 2021 general operating expenditures.

**Statement of activities**
Total expenses were $203,874,829: instruction $120,915,752, support services $67,702,339, community services $6,324,376, interest $4,533,849, food services $2,416,697, athletics $1,700,708, and other debt costs $281,108. Charges for services totaled $1,802,535 and operating grants and contributions $52,855,894, leaving net expense of $(149,216,400). General revenue of $144,318,096 included property taxes of $39,308,501 for general purposes, $17,345,162 for debt service, and $4,152,751 for capital projects, plus $81,687,900 of unrestricted state aid. Change in net position was $(4,898,304).

**Fund results**
Governmental funds ended with a combined fund balance of $57,844,378, a decrease of $6.2 million. Special revenue fund balance rose from $2.8 million to $3.1 million; debt service funds fell $1.2 million; capital project funds fell $12.1 million. Sinking fund millage collections were $4.1 million.

**Budget**
The final General Fund budget was amended in June 2021, raising budgeted revenue $21.7 million. Bonds outstanding were $130,280,000 plus $7,678,963 of unamortized premium. The district issued $40,425,000 of refunding bonds and advance refunded $37,860,000 of 2012 and 2014 bonds, reducing debt service over seven years by approximately $4,064,000 for an economic gain of about $2,559,000. Standard & Poor's affirmed the AA/Stable rating in May 2021.

**Pension and OPEB**
Pension contributions were $27,611,786 (including $11,658,202 of state UAAL stabilization funding) and OPEB contributions $6,980,805. Pension expense was $47,852,726; OPEB recovery was $860,940.

**What it is**
A multi-part packet supporting the award of a building lease for Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy (OCMW! Troy), operated by Troy School District. It combines a preliminary lease cost estimate memo, a lease rationale, the full RFP 9929 solicitation document, the announcement email and newspaper advertisement, the two vendor proposals, and SAM.gov registration search screenshots.

**Need for a new lease**
The district's lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400 expires October 31, 2021. The facility requires a 3-5 year lease to maintain operations of what the packet describes as the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, serving 17,000+ job seekers and hundreds of area businesses annually.

**Market comparison (Signature Associates, at no cost to the district)**

| Property | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| 3221 W. Big Beaver, Troy | $17.00/sq ft + electric |
| 3270 W. Big Beaver Road, Troy | $15.50/sq ft + electric |
| 2855 Coolidge Hwy, Troy | $17.50/sq ft + electric |

| 850 Stephenson Hwy, Troy | $13.00/sq ft + electric |

Moving costs are estimated to average $150,000.00 - $200,000.00, covering technology upgrades, server relocation, buildout, packing, furniture and other unexpected costs.

**Solicitation**
RFP 9929 was announced publicly Tuesday, August 3, 2021, posted to www.troy.k12.mi.us, emailed by Purchasing Supervisor Todd Hensley at 9:01:04 AM that day, and distributed through State of Michigan SIGMA VSS/DM to an additional 19 contacts. | Year | L Mason Capitani | SF | $/SF | Friedman Real Estate | SF | $/SF |

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Procurement packet assembled for the Troy School District Board of Education covering RFP 9929, Professional Office Space Lease, Oakland County Michigan Works, Troy Public Schools. Tabbed sections cover Preliminary Lease Cost, Lease Rationale, the RFP - Building Lease document, the Email to Vendors Announcing RFP, the Press Release/Newspaper Ad, the L Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate proposals, and SAM.gov entity searches.

**Need for a new lease.** Troy School District's (Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy) lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400 is set to expire on October 31, 2021. The facility needs a 3-5 year lease to maintain operations of the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, which provides workforce services to 17,000+ job seekers and hundreds of area businesses on a yearly basis.

**Cost reasonableness and market comparison.** Troy School District (Troy Michigan Works) used Signature Associates, at no cost to the district, to obtain quotes for comparable facilities and lease requirements. The 2021 quotes listed are: 3221 W. Big Beaver, Troy, MI at $17.00 per square foot plus electric; 3270 W. Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI at $15.50 per square foot plus electric; 2855 Coolidge Hwy, Troy, MI at $17.50 per square foot plus electric; 2800 Livernois Rd, Troy, MI at $17.95 per square foot plus electric; 850 Stephenson Hwy, Troy, MI at $13.00 per square foot plus electric; and 700 Tower Dr., Troy, MI at $17.95 - 18.95 per square foot plus electric.

**Moving costs.** The district estimates moving costs could average $150,000.00 - $200,000.00, including technology upgrades, moving servers, buildout of a new facility, moving and packing costs, furniture costs, and other unexpected moving-related costs.

**Public bid process.** RFP 9929 was announced publicly on Tuesday, August 3, 2021, with a newspaper announcement included in the packet, and made available on the district website, www.troy.k12.mi.us. The RFP was sent directly to Robbins Investments 550 LLC, Rob Krochmal, 248-867-3304, robk@surnow.com; L. Mason Capitani Corfac International, Mason Capitani, 248-637-7795, MLCapitani@lmcap.com; Winston-Traitel Realty, Inc, Jeff Raitt, 248-624-7200, jraitt@wtrealty.com; Friedman Integrated Real Estate Solutions, Robert Gagniuk, 248-830-9400, robert.gagniuk@freg.com; and Thomas Duke Realty, Rachel Pannell, 248-476-3700, info@thomasduke.com. The district additionally used State of Michigan SIGMA VSS/DM, which included an additional 19 contacts. L. Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate submitted proposals by the August 18th, 2021 deadline. The announcement email was sent by Todd Hensley on Tuesday, August 3, 2021 at 9:01:04 AM to info@thomasduke.com, Robk@surnow.com, MLCapitani@Imcap.com, Greggory.Kent@freg.com and jraitt@wtrealty.com, with the attachment RFP 9929 Oakland County MI Works Office Space.pdf.

**RFP terms.** Troy Schools accepted firm, sealed proposals to establish a five-year building lease beginning November 1, 2021 and ending October 31, 2026, annually renewed. Proposals and two copies marked RFP 9929 MI Works Professional Office Space Lease were due no later than 1:00 p.m., Wednesday, August 18, 2021 at the Purchasing Department, Troy School District, 1140 Rankin, Troy, Michigan 48083, where bids would be publicly opened and read aloud. Questions were accepted in writing only, due no later than noon Wednesday, August 11, 2021, by fax to 248.823.4077 or email to PurchasingOffice@troy.k12.mi.us. The stated timeline lists RFP released Tuesday, August 3, 2021; pre-proposal questions due Wednesday, August 11, 2021 at noon; proposals due Wednesday, August 18, 2021 at 1:00 PM; and Board award September 2021. Proposals remain firm for a minimum of 180 days after opening. The undersigned agrees to execute a contract if notified of acceptance within thirty days after opening, and bids may not be withdrawn until after forty-five (45) days after receipt of bids. Termination of the Agreement upon regulatory order requires thirty (30) days written prior notice.

Vendors must submit sworn and notarized familial disclosure statements covering relationships with any member of the Troy School Board or the Troy Schools Superintendent, plus a completed Iran Economic Sanctions affidavit under Michigan Public Act No. 517 of 2012. A false certification carries a civil penalty of not more than $250,000.00 or two (2) times the amount of the contract, whichever is greater, plus investigation costs and reasonable attorney fees, and ineligibility to bid for three (3) years. Insurance requirements include satisfactory Workers' Compensation coverage and General Liability and Property Damage Insurance of at least $1,000,000.00 per occurrence and $1,000,000.00 in aggregate, plus automobile insurance of at least $1,000,000.00. Registration on www.sam.gov is required, and vendors must certify they are not debarred from doing business with the federal government. The district is a tax-exempt entity except where the project makes enhancements or additions to real property, and is subject to the Michigan Freedom of Information Act.

**Scoring criteria and specifications.** Each responsive proposal is scored on a 100 point scale: Location and proximity to client population, 50 points; Cost Reasonableness, 25 points; Lease requirements, 25 points. Specifications require no less than 7000 square feet and no more than 8,000 square feet, free public parking including at least one handicapped space, public transportation access within walking distance, at least 4 bathrooms, a kitchen facility with running water, and accessibility for internet, wireless and telephone technology. The contract must permit termination without penalty costs or fees should federal funds or other applicable funding sources become unavailable.

**Lease cost comparison.** L Mason Capitani proposed 7,494 square feet at $14.00 per square foot for a 2021-22 lease cost of $104,916.00; $14.25 and $106,789.50 for 2022-23; $14.75 and $110,536.00 for 2023-24; $15.00 and $112,410.00 for 2024-25; and $15.25 and $114,283.50 for 2025-26. Friedman Real Estate proposed 7,000 - 10,000 square feet at $15.00 per square foot for $105,000.00 - $150,000.00 in 2021-22; $15.30 for $107,100.00 - $153,000.00 in 2022-23; $15.61 for $109,270.00 - $156,100.00 in 2023-24; $15.92 for $111,440.00 - $159,200.00 in 2024-25; and $16.24 for $113,680.00 - $162,400.00 in 2025-26. Notes state the first year is $15.00 per square foot with a 2% annual increase shown in the quote, additional amortized leasing costs to be determined, that all bid amounts are plus electric and include daily janitorial services, and that L Mason Capitani costs include maintenance (CAM) costs while Friedman's are additional.

**Bid scoring.** Bids were reviewed and scored by a committee of Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor, Troy School District; Denise Van Hee, Director, Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy; and Cheryl Schubeck, Program Coordinator, Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy. Final scores reflect the average of all three scores in each category. On Location/Proximity to client Population (50 pts), L Mason Capitani received 45 for close proximity to a bus stop and two expressways (696 and I-75) and the Troy/Clawson/Madison Heights population served, while Friedman received 40 for close proximity to a bus stop and one expressway (I-75) and the Troy/Rochester Hills population. On Cost Reasonableness (25 pts), L Mason Capitani received 25 for an overall rate of $14 - $15 per square foot with maintenance included, below market rates, and no cost for moving expenses, buildouts or technology; Friedman received 20 for a rate of $15 - $16.24 per square foot in line with market rates but higher than current costs, with maintenance additional and additional moving and technology expenses. Both received 25 on Lease Requirements (25 pts), each meeting space, parking, kitchen and bathroom requirements and allowing lease termination with notice for financial reasons. Totals were 95 for L Mason Capitani and 85 for Friedman. All three committee members scored L Mason Capitani 45/25/25 and Friedman Real Estate 40/20/25. The summary concludes L Mason Capitani received the highest evaluation score and is the most reasonable and cost-effective option, with a proposed rate per square foot below current market rates and moving described as very costly.

**Friedman proposal detail.** Dated Aug 18, 2021 and presented by Robert Gagniuk, Real Estate Specialist, Client Solutions, robert.gagniuk@freg.com, 248.848.4093, ECODE 737, with Anya Eliassen copied, the Friedman Integrated Real Estate Solutions proposal covers North Troy Corporate Park, 5505 Corporate Drive, Troy, MI 48084. Oakland County Health Network (OCHN) is the owning entity, leasing excess office and meeting space to a network of providers. The proposal covers +/- 7,000 to 10,000 square feet on the second or third floor, with the second floor total available at +/- 23,507 SF and the third floor at +/- 7,710 SF; measurements are per ANSI/BOMA 2010. The term commences upon substantial completion with a target date of October 1, 2021, with early entry permitted thirty (30) days prior for FF&E installation. The rental rate goal is at or below $15.00/RSF plus suite electric, with Year 1 at $15.00/SF + E, amortized leasing costs TBD and 2% annual increases; base rent includes base year expenses, base year real estate taxes and five (5) nights per week of janitorial service. Tenant pays its pro-rata share of increases over the 2021 calendar base year, with a gross-up if the building is less than ninety-five percent (95%) leased. The security deposit equals one month's base rent based on the third month of the term. Parking is free at a ratio of 5.86/1000 SF, 748 spaces in total including 19 barrier free spaces. The building offers 24/7 access 365 days per year, a pneumatic VAV HVAC system with computer-controlled energy management, high-speed fiber optic data, a renovated lobby, full gym and locker rooms, cafe and sundry shop. Listed area amenities include Jimmy Johns, Cedar Grille, Red Robin, Kirby's Coney Island, Papa Romano Pizza, Bagel Factory, Sushi Do, Embassy Suites, Courtyard Marriott, Drury Inn & Suites, Detroit Marriott, MET Hotel, MJR Digital Cinemas, Somerset Mall, Ridgedale Players, Northfield Market and Sylvan Glen Golf Course. Friedman's headquarters is 34975 W. Twelve Mile Rd, Farmington Hills, MI 48331, 248.324.2000. The proposal remains in effect only until October 1, 2021 and is not contractually binding.

Lease Rationale - 2021, prepared by Troy School District (Troy Michigan Works) to justify the office lease recommendation for Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy brought to the Board of Education.

**Need for new lease.** Troy School District's (Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy) lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400 is set to expire on October 31, 2021. The facility will need to secure a 3-5 year lease to maintain operations of the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, which provides workforce services to 17,000+ job seekers and hundreds of area businesses on a yearly basis.

**Cost reasonable / cost comparison.** Troy School District (Troy Michigan Works) utilized Signature Associates to assist with lease cost estimates, and Signature Associates obtained quotes for comparable facilities and lease requirements at no cost to the district. The 2021 quotes are: 3221 W. Big Beaver, Troy, MI at $17.00 per square foot plus electric; 3270 W. Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI at $15.50 per square foot plus electric; 2855 Coolidge Hwy, Troy, MI at $17.50 per square foot plus electric; 2800 Livernois Rd, Troy, MI at $17.95 per square foot plus electric; 850 Stephenson Hwy, Troy, MI at $13.00 per square foot plus electric; and 700 Tower Dr., Troy, MI at $17.95 - 18.95 per square foot plus electric.

**Moving costs.** The district estimates that moving costs could average $150,000.00 - $200,000.00. This includes technology upgrades, moving servers, buildout of a new facility, moving and packing costs, furniture costs, and other unexpected moving-related costs.

**RFP - public bid.** Troy School District (Troy Michigan Works) announced RFP 9929, Professional Office Space Lease Oakland County Michigan Works Troy Public Schools, publicly on Tuesday, August 3, 2021, with a newspaper announcement included in the packet, and made it available on the Troy School District website, www.troy.k12.mi.us. The RFP was sent directly to the following area vendors: Robbins Investments 550 LLC, Rob Krochmal, 248-867-3304, robk@surnow.com; L. Mason Capitani Corfac International, Mason Capitani, 248-637-7795, MLCapitani@lmcap.com; Winston-Traitel Realty, Inc, Jeff Raitt, 248-624-7200, jraitt@wtrealty.com; Friedman Integrated Real Estate Solutions, Robert Gagniuk, 248-830-9400, robert.gagniuk@freg.com; and Thomas Duke Realty, Rachel Pannell, 248-476-3700, info@thomasduke.com. In addition, TSD utilized State of Michigan SIGMA VSS/DM, which included an additional 19 contacts. The memo states that L. Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate submitted proposals by the August 20th, 2021 deadline.

**Lease costs.** The comparison table sets out, for each vendor, annual lease cost, square feet, and cost per square foot. L Mason Capitani: 2021-22 lease cost $104,916.00 for 7,494 square feet at $14.00 per square foot; 2022-23 $106,789.50 at 7,494 square feet and $14.25; 2023-24 $110,536.00 at 7,494 square feet and $14.75; 2024-25 $112,410.00 at 7,494 square feet and $15.00; 2025-26 $114,283.50 at 7,494 square feet and $15.25. Friedman Real Estate: 2021-22 $105,000.00 - $150,000.00 for 7,000 - 10,000 square feet at $15.00 per square foot; 2022-23 $107,100.00 - $153,000.00 for 7,000 - 10000 square feet at $15.30; 2023-24 $109,270.00 - $156,100.00 for 7,000 - 10,000 square feet at $15.61; 2024-25 $111,440.00 - $159,200.00 for 7,000 - 10,000 square feet at $15.92; 2025-26 $113,680.00 - $162,400.00 for 7,000 - 10,000 square feet at $16.24. Repeated table footnotes state: first year $15.00 per square foot, with rates above indicating a 2% annual increase shown in the quote, plus additional amortized leasing costs TBD; all bid amounts are 'plus' electric and include daily janitorial services; and L Mason Capitani costs include maintenance (CAM) costs while Friedman's are additional.

**Scoring of bids.** Bids were reviewed and scored by a committee comprised of Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor, Troy School District; Denise Van Hee, Director, Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy; and Cheryl Schubeck, Program Coordinator, Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy. Comments supporting individual scores were summarized and included in the chart, and it was determined that final scores would reflect the average of all three scores submitted for each category. All three committee members scored L Mason Capitani 45/25/25 and Friedman Real Estate 40/20/25.

On Location/Proximity to client Population (50 pts), L Mason Capitani scored 45, cited for close proximity to a bus stop and two expressways (696 and I-75) and closeness to the Troy/Clawson/Madison Heights population served; Friedman scored 40, cited for close proximity to a bus stop and one expressway (I-75) and closeness to the Troy/Rochester Hills population served. On Cost Reasonableness (25 pts), L Mason Capitani scored 25, with an overall rate per square foot of $14 - $15 with maintenance costs included described as below market rates and no cost for moving expenses, buildouts or technology; Friedman scored 20, with an overall rate per square foot described as in line with market rates but higher than current costs at $15 - $16.24 per square foot, maintenance costs additional, buildout costs included, and additional expenses to be incurred for moving and technology. On Lease Requirements (25 pts), both scored 25, each meeting requirements of the lease including space, parking, kitchen and bathrooms, and each allowing lease termination with notice for financial reasons. Total Points (100 pts) were 95 for L Mason Capitani and 85 for Friedman.

**Summary.** Based on the outcome of the scoring of the submitted proposals, Troy School District (Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy) determined that the proposal submitted by L Mason Capitani is the most reasonable and cost-effective option at this time, that the proposed rate per square foot is below current market rates, and that it would be very costly to move.

It was carried on the February 23, 2021 board agenda as an updated version.

**Program framing.** Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities; participation in Schools of Choice is optional for districts; and the degree and extent of participation are determined at the local level, including application enrollment dates, grade levels and building assignment.

**Subgroup composition.** English Learners numbered 53 among SOC students, 16.26% with a change of -2.84%, and 1286 among non-SOC students, 26.24% with a change of -2.89%. **Kindergarten and First Grade enrollment history.** The presentation lists district Kindergarten and First Grade counts by year: 2008-2009, 775 and 830; 2009-2010, 739 and 817; 2010-2011, 752 and 785; 2011-2012, 727 and 832; 2012-2013, 768 and 795; 2013-2014, 766 and 814; 2014-2015, 700 and 787; 2015-2016, 755 and 728; 2016-2017, 798 and 769; 2017-2018, 812 and 845; 2018-2019, 800 and 871; 2019-2020, 792 and 845; and 2020-2021, 734 and 785, with the Kindergarten figure noted as including PreK (Developmental Kindergarten).

**Projected sibling preference placement.** A survey was emailed to current Schools of Choice families requesting information on siblings who would be eligible for Kindergarten, First Grade, and sixth, seventh and eighth grade for the 2021-2022 school year. The responses identify 10 Kindergarten students planning to attend, 1 First Grade student, and 9 Middle School students across sixth, seventh and eighth grade combined.

**Factors considered.** The February 2, 2021 memorandum lists the factors weighed in framing the recommendation: current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of Schools of Choice siblings who would be age-eligible to enter the district in 2021-2022 if a decision is made to admit a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students under Schools of Choice; and available elementary classrooms.

**Recommendations.** After analyzing that data, the administration recommends that the district use Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining the number of Schools of Choice students to admit for the 2021-2022 school year; accept SOC applications for 50 Kindergarten, 50 First Grade and 20 Middle School students, noting that based on the number of kindergarten applications received for the 2020-2021 school year the district anticipates attracting many more than 50 applicants, which would allow the district to admit 50 kindergarteners initially with the option of admitting additional students, if space allows, in the third week of August; and place middle school students in a building according to available space.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held February 15, 2022 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. before an audience of approximately 80. The Board adopted resolutions 22-015 through 22-026, each on a 7 to 0 vote, covering Principal Appreciation Month, the consent agenda, a new hire, open-enrollment closures, Schools of Choice numbers, several construction and technology awards, an IDEA Full Funding Act resolution, and a MASB ballot. The largest single action was the Site Work Paving Program awarded to Nagle Paving at a total of $2,048,607.75 from the Building Site Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund. The meeting adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, February 15, 2022, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Also present: Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson; Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, and West. Approximately 80 members of the audience attended. Adjourned 9:03 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.

**Recognitions**
Fall 2021 All-State Athletes were named across boys tennis, boys soccer, and girls golf. Athletic Director Tim Fulcher recognized the Troy High School Boys Tennis Team as MHSAA Division 1 State Champions for fall 2021 and presented certificates. The Board honored Melissa Verduyn, Systems Analyst/Admin Webmaster, for artwork visualizing the District pillars of World Class; Kerry Birmingham introduced her and presented a framed photograph of her artwork plus a certificate of appreciation.

Official minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held February 15, 2022 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, and West. There were approximately 80 members of the audience. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and bear the initials GH/jh.

RECOGNITION - ALL-STATE ATHLETES FALL 2021. The following students received the distinction of being named All-State Athletes in their respective sports: Srihari Ananthalwan (Boys Tennis), Aiden Baraiac (Boys Soccer), Derek Blackwell (Boys Tennis), Matthew Gawthrop (Boys Soccer), Rintaro Goda (Boys Tennis), Ryan Gruca (Boys Soccer), Mayank Gudi (Boys Tennis), Aryan Gupta (Boys Tennis), Olivia Hemmila (Girls Golf), John Palomino (Boys Soccer), Rishi Shetty (Boys Tennis), Nikhil Tatineni (Boys Tennis), Andrew Wang (Boys Tennis), Ava Weeks (Girls Golf), and Nicholas Worrell (Boys Soccer).

TROY HIGH BOYS TENNIS STATE CHAMPIONS. Director of Athletics Mr. Tim Fulcher recognized the Troy High School Boys Tennis Team for being named MHSAA Division 1 State Champions for the fall of 2021. Athletes called up to receive a certificate and congratulations were Haresh Anand (Sophomore), Srihari Ananthalwan (Junior), Pranav Bellad (Senior), Derek Blackwell (Sophomore), Yashwant Dubbaka (Junior), Aryan Gupta (Senior), Dhruv Gupta (Freshman), Sai Rushil Kagithala (Junior), Shalin Kakasani (Senior), KyungJin Kim (Sophomore), Nishit Palepu (Sophomore), Eric Rymkiewicz (Senior), Zachary Saad (Senior), Joshua Samuelsen (Sophomore), Rishi Shetty (Senior), Sachin Sridhar (Senior), Nikhil Tatineni (Senior), and Andrew Wang (Senior). Srihari Ananthalwan and Aryan Gupta were noted as Flight State Champions at #2 Doubles; Pranav Bellad and Zachary Saad were noted as Flight State Champions at #3 Doubles.

TSD MISSION MOMENT. The Board honored Melissa Verduyn, Systems Analyst/Admin Webmaster, who works in both the Technology Department and on the creative team. When the District began the process to evolve the characteristics of a world class school district, it ran into challenges producing a visual image similar to the pillars that could accurately communicate the vision; Verduyn brought it together in a way that helps the community understand and connect. Kerry Birmingham introduced Melissa, described her contributions, and presented her with a framed photograph of her artwork along with a certificate of appreciation.

PRINCIPAL APPRECIATION MONTH, RESOLUTION 22-015. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Hammond. The resolution recited that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 school principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between school and community; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals; and that during February the District joins educators, parents and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of the importance of educational leadership. It resolved that the Troy Board of Education officially recognizes February as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL CONSENT AGENDA, RESOLUTION 22-016. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne to approve items A, B, C, and D: minutes of the January 4, 2022 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the January 18, 2022 Board of Education Organizational and Regular Meeting; Treasurer's Report for December 2021; and cancellation of the March 12, 2022 Winter Retreat together with rescheduling of the July 19 Board Meeting to July 26, 2022, to be held at 9:00 a.m. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

PERSONNEL, RESOLUTION 22-017. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff to approve the elementary and secondary personnel recommendation, a new hire, Samantha Morgan. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

CURRICULUM - SCHOOLS CLOSED TO OPEN ENROLLMENT FOR 2022-2023, RESOLUTION 22-018. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, adopting a resolution to close Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools as well as Athens and Troy High Schools to open enrollment for the 2022-2023 school year, with the exception of not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High and currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2022-2023 school year. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

SCHOOLS OF CHOICE REPORT. Ms. Griffor shared that the Board had the opportunity to review the Schools of Choice data and information at the March 1, 2022 Board of Education Workshop, and that the Board would be asked to pass a resolution approving the suggested Schools of Choice numbers for the 2022-2023 school year.

SCHOOLS OF CHOICE 105 AND 105C, RESOLUTION 22-019. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. Exercising the option permitted by Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, the Board will accept applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2022-2023 school year for eighteen (18) kindergarten, three (3) first grade, and sixteen (16) total 6th through 8th grade nonresident students who attend a school district within or outside of Oakland County if that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Mrs. Hammond commented that she appreciates the District bringing the number of Schools of Choice students down from what it was years ago.

BUSINESS - SITE WORK PAVING PROJECTS, RESOLUTION 22-020. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Hauff, awarding the Site Work Paving Program bid and approving the amount as an expenditure of the Building Site Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund. Nagle Paving: Hamilton (main parking lot and drives) $524,990.00; Martell (drains, paving and retention pond) $562,990.00; Wass (parking lot, receiving drive, entrance loop) $567,125.00; Facilities and Operations $295,950.00; Contingency $97,552.75; TOTAL $2,048,607.75. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Mr. Hauff inquired as to when the paving projects would be completed; Mr. West indicated they should be finished by June 17th.

ASBESTOS ABATEMENT PROJECT, RESOLUTION 22-021. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Hammond, awarding the asbestos abatement bid to Quality Environmental in the amount of $85,600.00, approved as an expenditure from the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

NETWORK FIREWALL REPLACEMENT, RESOLUTION 22-022. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, awarding the network firewall replacement and approving the amount as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. Delta Networks base bid $327,353.04; Contingency $16,367.65; TOTAL $343,720.69. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

FIBER CONNECTION TO TLC, RESOLUTION 22-023. Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Dr. Philippart, awarding fiber connectivity services and approving the amount as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. Fiber Link, Inc. base bid $74,562.60; Make Ready Allowance $63,000.00; TOTAL $137,562.60. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

REPLACEMENT OVENS - ATHENS, RESOLUTION 22-024. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mrs. Anne, awarding the purchase of two UNOX ovens to Stafford Smith in the amount of $58,524.00, approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

STUDENT REPRESENTATIVE REPORTS. Sarayu Bethamcherla reported for Troy High School; Alyssa McLarty for Troy College and Career High School; Yara Mashal for International Academy-East; and Sasha Palmkoeck for Athens High School.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). President Schmidt described how Public Participation would be conducted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines for public comment. Speakers: Mrs. Katie MacFarland, TSD parent and resident, on the difference between equity and equality; Kristina Sosnoski, TSD parent and resident, on allowing parents to volunteer in classrooms again; Mrs. Kacy Bailey, parent of two students, on curriculum being taught in the District; Mr. Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent, on media content in school media centers; Mr. Christopher Henne, TSD parent, on diversity, equity and inclusion and arming kids with tools to be good quality citizens; B.J. Lennon, TSD parent, on the mask mandates being lifted; Mrs. Diana Magiera, TSD parent, on mask enforcements and effects on children; Stephanie Margilaj, TSD parent, on explicit books in school libraries; Kelly Jones, TSD parent, on the use of pronouns as a way to show respect; Dr. Stephanie Mikulski, TSD parent, on the mask requirement being discontinued prematurely; Ms. Ashleigh Jennings, TSD parent, on lifting the mask mandate and whether past mitigation measures will be reinstated; and Susan Tompkins, TSD resident, on masks and how teachers struggle to help students read with masks on.

OTHER - RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF IDEA FULL FUNDING ACT, RESOLUTION 22-025. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Wilson. The resolution recited that the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act was first enacted in 1975 to help ensure all students with disabilities have access to a free appropriate public education; that with IDEA's enactment the United States Congress committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost of special education, promising up to 40 percent of the national average per pupil expenditure, currently estimated at $13,828 by the U.S. Department of Education; that more than 45 years after enactment the current federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent; that Troy and many other districts educate a growing number of children with disabilities now numbering more than seven million; that districts face increased demand for greater resources, including for students with multiple disabilities whose individual education plans require more resources; and that with each increase in the IDEA child count boards adjust budgets, with some school districts dedicating forty percent or more of their general education budgets to special education services. The Board resolved to support the IDEA Full Funding Act authorizing a ten year plan to fully fund the federal share of IDEA, to urge Congress's strong bipartisan support and passage, and to remain committed to providing students with disabilities and their families the supports they need while acknowledging the intergovernmental partnership among local, state, and federal levels of government. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

2022 MASB BOARD OF DIRECTORS ELECTION, RESOLUTION 22-026. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne, casting the Board's ballot for Melandie Hines, Wayne Westland Community Schools, for Region 8, three-year term, on the 2022 Michigan Association of School Boards Board of Directors. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS. Dr. Philippart thanked the principals for their work and dedication. Mrs. Hammond echoed the sentiment and suggested parents wanting to volunteer reach out to their building principals. Mr. Gottlieb gave a shout out to teachers and students for the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab Passion Projects. Mrs. Anne congratulated Teacher of the Year nominees and winners and mentioned visiting the STEMI truck at Troy High and student interest. Mr. Hauff announced that parents with a child who will be 5 by September 1, 2022 should enroll early for kindergarten. Dr. Wilson echoed other members and mentioned the STEMI truck and how high school students get middle school students excited about learning. Dr. Machesky congratulated the athletes, Melissa Verduyn, and the principals, noted the District celebrated four Teacher of the Year winners the prior weekend, and thanked the TFEE for its monetary award, the TEA for its support, and Suburban Collection for a 2-year auto lease. Mr. Schmidt gave a shout out to Bill Turner for organizing the STEMI truck visit, and announced the next Board Workshop for March 1st at 6:00 p.m. at the Services Building and the next Board Meeting for March 15th at 7:00 p.m., also at the Services Building.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

Vendor sales deck from Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. titled Managed Detection and Response and Managed Security Awareness Training Proposal Overview, dated 3/21/22 and carried on the Troy School District Board agenda as item 3.a. The cover slide is marked Classification: Public; most interior slides carry the notice Classification: Confidential with copyright lines for 2020 and 2021 Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. Presented To: Beth Soggs, IT Director, and Alan Wilson, Network Manager. Prepared By: Nick Hankins, Account Executive, Arctic Wolf, and Chris Pittman, Sr. Systems Engineer, Arctic Wolf. People Driven, the partner organization, is represented by Bryan Teipel, President, and Dave Benham, Solution Architect. The proposal contents are enumerated as six sections: Executive Summary, Current Assessment, Why Arctic Wolf, Security Risk Quantification, Pricing Proposal, and Partnership and Enablement.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY. The strategic initiative is stated as Enhance Security and Visibility. The problem statement holds that Troy Schools has a distributed network across multiple physical buildings with most traffic backhauled to the central hub, making visibility across the environment and monitoring of network traffic a challenge; that Troy Schools has multiple security tools in place with limited staff to monitor and correlate alerts or identify and respond to potential malicious activity; and that a lack of a broad detection and response mechanism could prevent the ability to quickly identify, contain and remediate sophisticated threats. The desired outcomes are to operationalize a full-feature SIEM solution leveraging existing IT and security controls, to obtain a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service, and to leverage a service-based solution that can identify, evaluate, and provide quarantine and remediation guidance for threat indicators in real time. The proposed solution is Arctic Wolf's security operations as-a-concierge service ingesting Troy Schools environmental telemetry to perform 24x7x365 observations, investigations, and incident response guidance; an open, vendor-agnostic SIEM platform ingesting standardized log sources and live network traffic analysis; and three dedicated Security Operations FTEs using the Arctic Wolf Cloud Platform for proactive threat hunting and continuous improvement.

CURRENT ASSESSMENT. Current challenges reported from the Troy team: IT and security resources are constrained and the cost and complexity of building a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is probably unrealistic; endpoint and network security tools are in place and seasoned security professionals are desired for guidance in environmental hardening and continuous improvement; and there is interest in human-led, proactive threat hunting over basic alert-response services. Negative business impacts listed include risk from cyber attack, reactive response distracting burdened IT staff from existing initiatives, and inability to identify dormant vulnerabilities and threats. Value drivers are described as Benchmark Your Business, Team Enhancement, Faster Intrusion Detection, and Harden Your Environment, the latter via the CST evaluating vulnerability and risk data and presenting on-demand executive reports and personalized risk remediation plans.

SERVICE OFFERINGS. Managed Risk (Discover, Benchmark, Harden) is framed against the Center for Internet Security statement that 80% of breaches could have been prevented if the organization had met the top 5 CIS controls. Managed Detection and Response covers Detect, Respond, and Recover. Managed Cloud Monitoring covers Identify, Monitor, and Simplify, including unsecured S3 buckets and unauthorized cloud deployments, IaaS configuration risks, and SaaS indicators of compromise. Managed Security Awareness covers Engage, Measure, and Transform. A statistics band on the same slide prints the figures 47%, 80%, 85% and 70% alongside claims regarding incidents including a cloud component, threats preventable by meeting the top 5 CIS controls, data breaches resulting from employee actions, and new customer environments containing latent threats.

TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT MDR ARCHITECTURE. The scoped environment is stated as 1200 Users, 12,500 Student Users, 100 Servers, 1 300 Series Sensor, and 90 Day Log Retention, using AWN301 sensors and Secure Transport with API and platform integration to the Arctic Wolf Concierge Security Team. Monitored inputs include client monitoring agent and quarantine, firewall/UTM, Active Directory, server logs, anti-virus, Arctic Wolf Agent, DNS logs, HTTP and TLS, wireless APs, Cisco AMP for Endpoints, network monitoring with log collection and NTA, wireless networks, Windows event logs, system vulnerabilities, rootkit/compromise checks, process tables, installed patches, configuration benchmarks, asset information, and cloud monitoring of SaaS and IaaS.

WHY ARCTIC WOLF. Industry framing figures: 3,000 vendors, $120B total spend, and 3,950 reported breaches. Company facts: 1,200+ employees, 3,300+ customers, founded 2012. Audit and compliance drivers named are PCI DSS, FFIEC-NCUA, HIPAA, NIST 800-171, and 23 NYCRR 500. Better Protection statistics: Dwell Time 0:30, with the industry average time to identify an intrusion given as 206 days versus 30 minutes or less for Arctic Wolf; Phishing 18% of customers have phishing activity missed by email security but caught by Arctic Wolf; Advanced Threats 43% of customers have advanced threat activity missed by security tools; Account Takeover 70% of customers have some PII exposure, with 5.5% having plaintext passwords exposed online; and Unpatched Vulnerabilities 35% reduction in time to patch critical vulnerabilities after activating Arctic Wolf. The top five attack vectors listed are malware/ransomware, phishing, PUP adware, account hijacking, and unpatched outdated software. Citing the 2019 Ponemon Cost of Data Breach Incident Report, the deck prints 84 Days Mean Time to Contain (MTTC), 230 Days Mean Time to Identify (MTTI), and 314 DAYS. Citing Gartner, 70% of organizations are unable to process more than 60% of their security data, and the security skills gap through 2020 is given as 1.5M.

SECURITY OPERATIONS SCALE. The platform slide prints approximately 165M observations per week, approximately 765 investigations per week, and approximately 1-2 tickets per week, with an illustrative environment of 450 Users, 150 Servers, and 4 Sensors, flowing through Arctic Wolf Triage, the Concierge Security Team, a data lake and correlation database, threat intelligence and IOCs, and a real-time correlation engine.

SECURITY MONITORING BREAKDOWN. The general observation breakdown is given as Network/IDS 30%, SaaS/O365 15%, Active Directory/Domain Controllers 10%, Firewall 10%, EDR/AV 10%, Arctic Wolf Agent 10%, External Vulnerabilities 5%, Account Takeover 5%, and Other (VPN, Darktrace, Varonis) 5%. A comparison table asserts that NTA is included with the Arctic Wolf sensor while others offer NIDS/HIDS only, that asset inventory across endpoint and network is included, that vulnerability scanning is included, and that integrations, engagement with the CST, remote incident response, security guidance, custom rules, log ingestion and volume, log bandwidth, and security posture reviews are unlimited, with security posture reviews defaulting to once per month.

PRICING PROPOSAL. Arctic Wolf MDR is described as including a fully managed and hosted SIEM, 24x7 monitoring, a named Concierge Security Team, Managed Cloud Monitoring for O365 and Azure, monthly external vulnerability scanning, host-based isolation and managed containment, monthly and quarterly reporting, ad hoc reports on request, unlimited log volume and events per second, 90 days log retention, unlimited custom rules, and managed IDS. Arctic Wolf Service Assurance protects Troy Schools with up to $500,000 in financial assistance for a covered security event, itemized as Compliance $100,000, Ransomware and BEC $100,000, Cyber Legal Liability $250,000, and Business Income $50,000; eligibility requires purchasing MDR and Managed Awareness or Managed Risk and committing to standard terms of an annual contract paid upfront with an 8% annual renewal increase. A separate slide states a multi-year deal with all products is required to qualify for the $1,000,000 level. Arctic Wolf Managed Security Awareness includes a fully managed awareness program, awareness program coaching, multiple integration options, gamification, ongoing microlearning, integrated phishing simulations, 24x7 account takeover monitoring, and performance analytics.

District data on SAT college level reading readiness show Cohort 1 (2016-2018) at 82.47 in 9th grade, 83.50 in 10th, and 76.85 in 11th, a stated decrease of 5.62%, and Cohort 2 (2017-2019) at 86.80, 84.70, and 81.44, a stated decrease of 5.36%.
