https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Topic**
ELA Curriculum Review and Revision, Grades 9-12, 2021-2022, presented to the Troy Board of Education.

**Collectively Developed Priorities**
The need to effectively serve ALL students; recent SAT college level reading readiness data meriting consideration; addressing the gap between high and low performing students; adequate training for teachers in advancing readers; a priority placed on the blue and red pillars; protected practice time for reading, writing, and critical thinking; learning environments conducive to responsive teaching; building student independence in college and career readiness skills; a commitment to rich, student-centered discussion and critical thinking; and choice, rigor, and diversity of text selection in all courses.

**District Data: SAT College Level Reading Readiness**

| Cohort | 9th Grade | 10th Grade | 11th Grade | Stated change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cohort 1: 2016-2018 | 82.47 | 83.50 | 76.85 | Decrease of 5.62% |
| Cohort 2: 2017-2019 | 86.80 | 84.70 | 81.44 | Decrease of 5.36% |

**Rationale**
The presentation cites Michael Fullan et al (2006), Breakthrough, for the proposition that the old mission of schools was universal access to basic education plus university access for a small elite, and that whereas twenty years ago 95% of jobs were low-skilled, today those jobs constitute only 10% of the entire economy. The new mission is to get all students to meet high standards and equip them as lifelong learners. Capacities of the literate individual are excerpted from the Michigan Common Core State Standards: demonstrate independence; build strong content knowledge; respond to the varying demands of audience, task, purpose and discipline; comprehend as well as critique; value evidence; use technology and media strategically and capably; and come to understand other perspectives and cultures.

**Course Pathways**
Current trajectory, described as limited options and a linear path: 9 Lit and Comp, 10 Lit and Comp, 11 LC/Elective, 12 Lit and Comp, with an honors strand of 9 LC Honors, 10 LC Honors, 11 AP Language, 12 AP Literature. Preferred future, described as more options with all students prepared for choice: 9th Grade English in 2023-2024 and 10th Grade English in 2024-2025, opening into American Lit, World Lit, AP Language, AP Literature, and Electives.

**Workshop Model Experience**
The literacy journey runs from elementary through middle school to high school, with curricular coherence aligning to Workshop in elementary at 5th and 6th grade. Middle school teachers report that avid readers are plowing through books and reluctant readers are reading more than in past years, that students are writing more daily through jots, long writes and flash drafts, that current students are performing well and challenge themselves with higher level books through book clubs, and that students are more engaged and thinking deeply. Areas for growth identified by middle school colleagues are conferring, resources and professional development, and small group resources and professional development.

**Professional Development**
5 teachers participated in the Teachers College Writing Institute in July 2021. 8 teachers participated in the Teachers College HS Book Club Institute in December 2021. 11 teachers participated in a webinar with Penny Kittle and Kelly Gallagher in December 2021. A full day of PD was provided in August, led by fellow teachers. During the November late start, a TC Staff Developer led PD on using on-demand writing samples to inform small groups and conferring. 9th grade teachers and coaches continue to visit middle school classrooms. Coaches participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in March 2022 and secondary administrators in February 2022, both with TC Staff Developer Natalie Louis.

**Current Work and Next Steps**
A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team was created, prioritized skills for 9th grade, and outlined skills for all 6 units; the team has met twice to unpack vertical alignment of skills from 6-8, will visit middle school classrooms to observe through the lenses of 3 workshop commitments, and will spend time with a TC Staff Developer in lab settings receiving guidance for Units 1-3. The goal is to write 6 workshop-style, skill-based units to be piloted in 2022-2023. Next steps: summer learning through the Teaching Writing in High School Institute and a Summer Homegrown Institute on Creating Teacher Toolkits to Support a Wide-Range of Writers, followed by targeted piloting of 9th grade units in Fall 2022.

**Ask of the Board**
Target professional development to meet teacher needs, specifically centered around responsive teaching and differentiation at both middle school and high school, and continue to honor the workshop commitment of choice by funding access to fascinating texts.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board meeting PowerPoint presenting the English Language Arts Curriculum Review and Revision for Grades 9-12 during the 2021-2022 school year in the Troy School District, setting out why the high school ELA program should shift toward the reading and writing workshop model already implemented in the District's elementary and middle schools.

COLLECTIVELY DEVELOPED PRIORITIES. The presentation opens with a list of priorities developed collectively: the need to effectively serve ALL students; recent data in SAT college level reading readiness that merits consideration; addressing the gap between high and low performing students; adequate training for teachers in advancing readers; a priority placed on the blue and red pillars; protected practice time for reading, writing, and critical thinking; learning environments conducive to responsive teaching; building student independence in college and career readiness skills; a commitment to rich, student-centered discussion and critical thinking; and choice, rigor, and diversity of text selection in all courses.

DISTRICT DATA, DECREASE IN SAT COLLEGE LEVEL READING READINESS. Two cohorts are tracked. Cohort 1, spanning 2016-2018, shows 9th Grade 82.47, 10th Grade 83.50, and 11th Grade 76.85, labeled as a Decrease of 5.62%. Cohort 2, spanning 2017-2019, shows 9th Grade 86.80, 10th Grade 84.70, and 11th Grade 81.44, labeled as a Decrease of 5.36%.

RATIONALE AND RESEARCH BASE. The deck quotes the argument that study after study shows globalization and new information technologies have made it especially urgent for schools to chart a new mission. It cites Breakthrough by Michael Fullan and colleagues (2006) for the point that the old mission for schools was to provide universal access to basic education and then to provide a small elite with access to university education. It states that the world has changed: whereas twenty years ago 95% of jobs were low-skilled, today those jobs constitute only 10% of the entire economy. The new mission is described as getting all students to meet high standards of education and providing them with a lifelong education that does not have the built-in obsolescence of so much old-style curriculum but that equips them to be lifelong learners.

STANDARDS FRAMING. Excerpted from the Michigan Common Core State Standards, the presentation lists the capacities of the literate individual that students exhibit with increasing fullness and regularity as they advance through the grades and master the standards in reading, writing, speaking, listening, and language: demonstrate independence; build strong content knowledge; respond to the varying demands of audience, task, purpose and discipline; comprehend as well as critique; value evidence; use technology and media strategically and capably; and come to understand other perspectives and cultures.

CURRENT COURSE TRAJECTORY. The present high school pathway is characterized as limited options on a linear path. The general sequence runs 9 Lit and Comp, 10 Lit and Comp, 11 LC/Elective, and 12 Lit and Comp. The accelerated sequence runs 9 LC Honors, 10 LC Honors, 11 AP Language, and 12 AP Literature.

PREFERRED COURSE STRUCTURE. The preferred model is described as more options with all students prepared for choice. It begins with a redesigned 9th Grade English course in 2023-2024 followed by a redesigned 10th Grade English course in 2024-2025, after which students may select from American Lit, World Lit, AP Language, AP Literature, and Electives.

LITERACY JOURNEY AND CURRICULAR COHERENCE. The presentation traces the literacy journey from elementary to middle school to high school, noting curricular coherence that aligns with Workshop in elementary, with slides addressing 5th Grade and 6th Grade and the movement of Workshop into the middle school.

WHAT THE DISTRICT HAS LEARNED FROM WORKSHOP IN MIDDLE SCHOOL. The stated lessons are that the student is at the center of the work; that skills are at the forefront with content used to achieve those skills; that choice in reading and writing allows for the engagement necessary for growth; that time to practice is the hallmark of the workshop model; and that normalizing feedback in the moment to meet students where they are promotes progress for all.

POSITIVE ASPECTS REPORTED BY MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHERS. Teachers report that avid readers are plowing through books and reluctant readers are reading more than in past years. Students are writing more, with daily jots, long writes, or flash drafts, and fewer students sit and say they do not know what to write about; notebooks are filled with drafts, revisions, and edits. Current students are performing well, with some challenging themselves through reading higher level books, and teachers report doing a good job encouraging reading more difficult books through book clubs. Students are described as more engaged and thinking deeply about what they are reading.

AREAS FOR GROWTH IDENTIFIED BY MIDDLE SCHOOL COLLEAGUES. Three areas are named: conferring; resources and professional development; and small group resources and professional development.

WHAT TEACHERS NEED AS THE WORK EXTENDS TO HIGH SCHOOL, AND THE ASK OF THE BOARD. The presentation asks the Board to target professional development to meet teacher needs, specifically centered around responsive teaching and differentiation at both the middle school and high school levels, and to continue to honor the workshop commitment of choice by funding access to fascinating texts.

ONGOING SUPPORT FOR TEACHERS THROUGHOUT THE TRANSITION. 5 teachers participated in the Teachers College Writing Institute in July 2021. 8 teachers participated in the Teachers College HS Book Club Institute in December 2021. 11 teachers participated in a webinar with Penny Kittle and Kelly Gallagher in December 2021. A full day of professional development was provided in August and led by fellow teachers. During the November late start, a Teachers College Staff Developer led professional development on how to use on-demand writing samples to inform small groups and conferring. 9th grade teachers and coaches continue to visit middle school classrooms. Coaches participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in March 2022, and secondary administrators participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in February 2022. Teachers shared their learning with the 9-12 ELA team, and teachers learned more about engaging students in writing to increase volume. The Administrators' Day and the Coaches' Day were both conducted with Teachers College Staff Developer Natalie Louis.

CURRENT WORK WITH HIGH SCHOOL. A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team (CDT) was created. The team prioritized skills for 9th grade and outlined skills for all 6 units. The CDT will visit middle school classrooms to observe through the lenses of the 3 workshop commitments. The stated goal is to write 6 workshop-style, skill-based units that will be piloted in 2022-2023. The team has already met twice to unpack the vertical alignment of skills from grades 6 through 8. The CDT will spend time with a Teachers College Staff Developer in lab settings and receive guidance for Units 1-3. Summer learning for the team includes creating teacher toolkits to support a wide range of writers and a Teaching Writing in High School Institute. A slide is devoted to the 9th Grade CDT's work on vertical alignment of skills.

NEXT STEPS. Summer learning consists of the Teaching Writing in High School Institute and a Summer Homegrown Institute titled Creating Teacher Toolkits to Support a Wide-Range of Writers. For Fall 2022, the next step is targeted piloting of the 9th grade units.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY. Desired outcomes are to operationalize a full-feature SIEM solution leveraging existing IT and security controls, a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service, and a service-based solution providing quarantine and remediation guidance in real time. The proposed solution is Arctic Wolf's security operations as-a-concierge service ingesting Troy Schools environmental telemetry for 24x7x365 observations, investigations, and incident response guidance; an open, vendor-agnostic SIEM platform ingesting all standardized log sources plus live network traffic analysis; and three dedicated Security Operations FTEs providing proactive threat hunting and continuous improvement.

Challenges heard from the Troy team: IT and security resources are constrained and the cost and complexity to build a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is probably unrealistic; endpoint and network security tools are in place and seasoned security professionals are wanted to guide environmental hardening and continuous improvement; and there is interest in human-led, proactive threat hunting over basic alert-response and typical operational-level services. Closing slides cover Arctic Wolf customers, Q&A, and a comparison of approaches to security operations spanning SIEM, MSSP, EDR, MDR, and XDR, with Arctic Wolf claiming coverage across the security operations framework, use of existing or Arctic Wolf technology, visibility across endpoint, network, cloud, apps, identity and people, unlimited and unmetered data pricing, and having invented the Concierge Security Team.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Troy School District's Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 states the district's middle school philosophy, nine program goals, five graduate outcomes, and the complete course catalog for grades 6, 7 and 8. Sixth graders take five academic classes plus required every-other-day physical education, while seventh and eighth graders take four academic classes plus required half-year Health/Physical Education and Digital Applications 1.0. Algebra 1 Honors, Geometry Honors and World Language I are taken in eighth grade, each earning high school credit and counting toward the high school GPA. The 18-page guide also catalogs more than two dozen half-year and full-year electives in visual art, music, computer science, engineering, media and life skills.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Publication**
Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide, 2024-2025, 18 pages, presented to the Board of Education on February 11, 2025.

**Philosophy and Goals**
Troy middle schools provide a program that recognizes, accepts, respects and meets the diverse needs of young adolescents, characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation; a shared vision fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community. Nine goals are listed, covering developmentally appropriate programs, meeting the needs of a diverse student population, core-subject skills and knowledge, discovery of special interests and aptitudes, diversified cultural/social/civic/vocational/recreational experiences, guidance services promoting self-esteem and responsible behavior, community partnerships, transition from elementary to high school, and modeling healthy lifestyles.

**Outcomes**
Five student outcomes: a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen.

**Three-Year Overview**

| Grade | Academic load | Additional requirements |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Five academic classes | Physical Education EOD required; music students may add Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD, Art EOD |
| 7 | Four academic classes | Health/Physical Education half year; Digital Applications 1.0 half year; music option of Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year |
| 8 | Four academic classes | Music option of Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year for music students, two full-year classes for non-music students |

EOD is defined as Every Other Day.

**Grade 6 Courses**
Required: ELA 6, Language Arts 6, Mathematics 6 (or another math class), Physical Education 6, Science 6, Social Studies 6. Mathematics 6 is organized into ten units: Area and Surface Area; Introducing Ratios; Linear Relationships; Unit Rates and Percentages; Dividing Fractions; Arithmetic in Base Ten; Expressions and Equations; Rational Numbers; Data Sets and Distributions; Putting it all Together. Grade 6 electives meet every other day alternating with PE: Art 6, Band 6 or Orchestra 6, and 6th Grade Choir.

**Grade 7 Courses**
Digital Applications 1.0 (half year, required), English 7, Health and Physical Education 7 (half year, a ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with parental excusal permitted), Mathematics 7, Science 7, and Social Studies 7, which surveys ancient world history and geography from the beginning until around 1500.

**Grade 8 Courses**
Algebra 1 Honors (five critical areas), English 8, Geometry Honors (six critical areas), Mathematics 8, Science 8, and United States History 8, which surveys U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877. Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and the high school GPA.

**Electives**
Half-year electives for grades 7 and 8: 2D Visual Art, 3D Visual Art, Applied Engineering, Art Expressions, Ceramics, Communication Arts, Computer Programming, Computer Science Discoveries, Creation Lab, Digital Applications 2.0, Innovation Incubator, Life Skills, LINKS (teacher recommendation only), Money Matters, Science and Engineering Explorations, Theatre Arts, Video Technology, and Video Technology 2. Grade 7 full-year electives: Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, Graphic Design/Yearbook. Grade 8 electives: 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra, Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band, Physical Education, Symphonic Band, WEB Leadership, and World Language I in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page publication appearing on the Board of Education agenda of February 11, 2025. It opens with the district's middle school philosophy: Troy middle schools provide a program that creates an environment recognizing, accepting, respecting and meeting the diverse needs and characteristics of young adolescent students, committed to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' innate curiosity, desire to expand their environment, and need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation that is challenging, integrative and exploratory; a shared vision with all members of the educational community fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community members.

Nine Middle School Goals are enumerated. Goal 1: all programs will be developmentally appropriate. Goal 2: ensure all programs meet the needs of a diverse student population. Goal 3: ensure all students develop skills and knowledge in the core subject areas. Goal 4: provide opportunity to discover special interests, attitudes, aptitudes and abilities. Goal 5: provide diversified experiences in cultural, social, civic, vocational and recreational programs. Goal 6: provide guidance services and programs promoting self-esteem, independence and responsible behavior. Goal 7: provide opportunity to establish partnerships with the community. Goal 8: provide a transition from elementary to high school. Goal 9: provide a model for healthy lifestyles.

Five Middle School Outcomes follow: a self-directed learner who is responsible, enthusiastic, thinks independently and is open-minded and intellectually curious; a quality worker who designs a plan, applies resources, technologies and organizational strategies, creates products and performances, monitors development, maintains high standards and assesses results; a positive communicator; a collaborative and cooperative contributor who creates and sustains productive group relationships, respects the contributions of others, helps resolve conflicts and stays focused and task oriented; and an involved and visionary citizen who develops awareness of global issues, contributes to local and world communities, advocates for the environment and prepares to meet future challenges.

The three-year middle school overview specifies that all sixth graders take five academic classes; seventh and eighth graders each take four academic classes. Sixth grade requires Physical Education on an every-other-day (EOD) basis for both music and non-music students, with Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD and Art EOD listed as the alternating options. Seventh grade requires Health/Physical Education for a half year and Digital Applications 1.0 for a half year, plus, for music students, one of Concert Band (full year), Chamber Orchestra (full year) or Choir (full year); the elective load totals one full year, taken as two half-year classes or one full-year class. Eighth grade music students choose among Symphonic Band (full year), Advanced Orchestra (full year) and Choir (full year); non-music eighth graders carry an elective total of two full-year classes, taken as four half-year classes, two half-year classes plus one full-year class, or two full-year classes.

Grade 6 required courses are ELA 6 (full year), which studies literature of various genres and informational text including literary nonfiction with emphasis on inference from textual evidence, thematic and character development, claims and evidence, academic vocabulary and independent choice reading; Language Arts 6 (full year), covering narrative, informational and argumentative writing using mentor texts and the writing process; Mathematics 6 (full year, or another math class), covering ratio and rate, dividing fractions by fractions, negative numbers and variables; Physical Education 6 (full year EOD), run either as a yearlong every-other-day program or an everyday semester class; Science 6 (full year), with units on cells and heredity, ecology, Earth's changing surface, and species adaptation and survival; and Social Studies 6 (full year), a geography-based course covering physical and human geography, migration and settlement, culture and cultural diffusion, population and demographic changes, resource use, and trade and economic interdependence. Mathematics 6 lists ten units: Unit 1 Area and Surface Area; Unit 2 Introducing Ratios; Unit 3 Linear Relationships; Unit 4 Unit Rates and Percentages; Unit 5 Dividing Fractions; Unit 6 Arithmetic in Base Ten; Unit 7 Expressions and Equations; Unit 8 Rational Numbers; Unit 9 Data Sets and Distributions; Unit 10 Putting it all Together.

Grade 6 elective courses meet every other day, alternating with PE: Art 6 (full year EOD), Band 6 or Orchestra 6 (full year EOD, with fifth-grade band or orchestra or prior formal instruction expected), and 6th Grade Choir (full year EOD), which follows the National Core Arts Standards of Perform, Create, Respond and Connect.

Grade 7 required courses are Digital Applications 1.0 (half year), covering 21st Century and Web 2.0 online tools; English 7 (full year); Health and Physical Education 7 (half year), a combined ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with units countering messages encouraging tobacco, alcohol and other drug use and information on the spread of AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases, and with parents permitted to excuse their child from sessions on human sexuality and AIDS; Mathematics 7 (full year, or another math class), extending rates and ratios to proportional relationships and all rational numbers; Science 7 (full year), covering Earth's waters, weather and climate, astronomy, waves, energy, physical and chemical changes, and chemical properties; and Social Studies 7 (full year), focused on ancient world history and geography with content literacy, investigating human history from the beginning until around 1500.

Grade 8 courses are Algebra 1 Honors (full year, or another math class), a first-year high school algebra course for advanced students with five critical areas covering linear equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, regression techniques, exponential/quadratic/rational equations and systems, and specialized functions including absolute value, step and piecewise-defined; English 8 (full year); Geometry Honors (full year, or another math class) for advanced students who have completed Algebra 1 Honors, with six critical areas covering congruence and rigid motions, similarity and right triangle trigonometry, coordinate geometry, circles, geometric measurement in two and three dimensions, and geometric modeling; Mathematics 8 (full year, or another math class), covering linear relationships, linear equations in one and two variables, functions and irrational numbers; Science 8 (full year), covering energy, biogeochemical cycles, resources and human impacts, the rock cycle, Earth's interior, plate tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, hydrogeology, severe weather, Earth in space, the sun, Earth history and geologic time and climate change, including an online Moodle project; and United States History 8 (full year), surveying U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877, with detailed study of the American Revolution, formation of the national government, westward movement, and the Civil War and Reconstruction, and periodic study of Michigan history and U.S. foreign affairs. Both Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and are figured into the high school GPA.

Half-year elective courses for grades 7 and 8 are 2D Visual Art; 3D Visual Art (papier-mache, clay, batik and mixed media); Applied Engineering (stress analysis, mechanical engineering, renewable energy systems, aerodynamics, space and rocketry); Art Expressions; Ceramics (pinch, coil and slab construction); Communication Arts (public speaking, pantomime, roleplaying, interviews, listening skills, improvisation); Computer Programming (Introduction to JavaScript: Drawing and Animation, JavaScript: Games and Visualizations, HTML/CSS: Making Webpages, HTML/JS: Making Webpages Interactive, plus building and programming a robot); Computer Science Discoveries; Creation Lab (bridge building, soldering, coding, game creation, projectiles, S.T.E.A.M. focus); Digital Applications 2.0 (Adobe Creative Suite, video production, animation, digital imaging, Dreamweaver; prerequisite is successful completion of Digital Applications 1.0); Innovation Incubator, whose cornerstone is the Larson Innovation Shark Tank project in which teams pitch inventions to members of the Metro Detroit business community including market researchers, patent attorneys and engineers; Life Skills (food preparation and hand and machine sewing); LINKS, a peer-to-peer support program pairing general education students with students with Autism Spectrum Disorder and other special needs, by teacher recommendation only; Money Matters (Michigan Career Pathways, budgets, bank accounts, credit, interest, investing and responsible spending); Science and Engineering Explorations, which prepares work for competitions such as the Science and Engineering Fair of Metro Detroit (SEFMD); Theatre Arts, which includes a public performance; Video Technology, using Windows Movie Maker and Apple iMovie with live morning news broadcasts and media literacy and copyright ethics; and Video Technology 2.

Grade 7 full-year electives are Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, and Graphic Design/Yearbook, the latter connecting students with the Boulan Park School Community. Grade 8 electives are 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra (which requires many evening performances plus a Saturday performance at the MSBOA Orchestra Festival), Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band (by audition or teacher approval, with members also participating in a concert band ensemble), Physical Education, Symphonic Band (requiring many evening performances plus two Saturday performances including MSBOA Band Festival), WEB Leadership (Where Everyone Belongs, covering sixth grade orientation, school character and culture programs, charity opportunities and student mentoring), and World Language I. World Language I is a full-year, every-day course counting toward high school credit and the high school GPA, offered in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I; the guide warns the class may only be offered at the high school during 1st hour, that parents would need to provide transportation to the high school, and that a shuttle will bring students back to the middle school.

Meeting and Attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, October 19, 2021, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m.; adjournment was at 8:57 p.m. Present with Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson, plus Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, Carrier, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Fulcher, Brinks, Cottone, DiPonio, Godfrey, Whan and West. Approximately 90 members of the audience attended. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary; footers are marked "corrected JH."

Recognition
The TSD Mission Moment honored Hill Elementary School's schoolwide "Color Run" of Friday, October 1st, designed to be inclusive of students with sensory issues; Principal Shari Pawlus and her PTO board members received a certificate. Resolution 21-081 commended seventy-four 2022 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists; per the resolution, more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the program and only 16,000 seniors are selected as semifinalists, by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT with comparable SAT scores. Copies were to be presented at a reception on November 3rd.

Actions Taken

| Res. | Item | Moved / Supported | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21-081 | 2022 National Merit Semifinalists resolution | — | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 21-082 | Consent agenda items A, B, C | Hauff / Gottlieb | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 21-083 | Accept audited 2021 financial statements | Wilson / Philippart | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 21-084 | Operating-All (Hold-Harmless) millage amendment | Philippart / Anne | Yes 7, No 0 |

Consent agenda 21-082 covered minutes of the September 7, 2021 Board Workshop, minutes of the September 21, 2021 Board Meeting, and the Treasurer's Report - August 2021.

Business
2020/2021 Audit: Ms. Donna Hanson and Mr. Michael Walsh of Plante Moran presented the audit of the 2020-2021 fiscal year, a draft of which had been detailed at the October 5, 2021 Board Workshop. There were no findings or questioned costs. Governmental funds revenue and expenditures, student population and foundation allowance were reviewed.

Millage amendment: The June 15, 2021 Budget Appropriations Resolution had authorized 4.4575 mills on Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal Properties and 13.5425 mills on all Non-Homestead Properties, a total levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes. The FY22 state school aid act, 2021 PA 48 (HB 4411), reduces hold-harmless (OPR ALL) millage; under section 1211 of the state school code per-pupil hold-harmless revenue is limited to the difference between the district's foundation allowance and $8,700. The amended 2021 Tax Rate Request (Form L-4029) sets a Principal Residence request of 3.3878 mills, 1.1591 of them levied December 1, 2021, and a Non-Homestead operating request of 14.6122 mills, 7.8409 of them levied on the December 1, 2021 levy date, and goes to the Oakland County Clerk and City of Troy Clerk.

Public Comment and Reports
Non-agenda speakers were split between opposition to and support for the mask mandate and Covid protocols, with further comment on library books, parental rights, a Schroeder Elementary drop-off incident, the Covid Family Guidebook and the "Moms for Liberty" organization. Student representatives Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Sasha Palmkoeck (Athens High School) and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School) reported; Alyssa McLarty (Troy College and Career High School) was not in attendance. Additions & Deletions, agenda-item public communication, Personnel and Curriculum were all "None."

Other
Board members congratulated Rick West and the Business Office for the audit. Dr. Machesky reported the Facilities Review Committee (FRC) held its first meeting, comprised of 54 community members and three Board members. Mr. Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for Tuesday, November 9th at 6:00 p.m. and the next regular Board Meeting for Tuesday, November 16th at 7:00 p.m., both at the Services Building.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Corrected minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Troy, Michigan, held October 19, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Every page footer carries the notation "Board of Education Meeting [page] October 19, 2021 - corrected JH," identifying this as the corrected version of the October 19 minutes. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

Call to Order and Attendance
President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, Carrier, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Fulcher, Brinks, Cottone, DiPonio, Godfrey, Whan and West. There were approximately 90 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:57 p.m.

Recognition - TSD Mission Moment: Hill Elementary School "Color Run"
Hill Elementary students participated in a schoolwide Color Run event on Friday, October 1st. The Fun Run was specifically designed to be inclusive and mindful of students who might have sensory issues. The Color Run involves colorful chalk being thrown into the air and decorating the shirts of those running by, and Fun Runs typically involve lots of cheering, music, loud audio and visual stimulants. For a portion of Hill's Color Run the music was turned off and cheering consisted of hands in the air and thumbs up instead of clapping and raised voices; the quiet allowed students who have sensory issues to fully enjoy the Fun Run, and the entire 5th grade was there to quietly but enthusiastically cheer them on. The minutes characterize the event as an example of the district's Red Pillar (Equity & Well-Being) "at its finest," thanking Hill Elementary for demonstrating that "ALL means ALL in the TSD." The Board invited Principal Shari Pawlus up along with her PTO board members to receive a certificate of recognition.

Recognition and Resolution 21-081 - 2021-22 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists
The minutes state that more than one million students nationwide, from some 21,000 high schools, entered the National Merit Scholarship Program, but only 16,000 of these seniors are selected to be semifinalists. The Board passed a resolution to commend and congratulate the district's seventy-four National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists, named as: Prisha Agnihotri, Frederick Aldinger, Sreenand Anumolu, Akshat Arya, Seo Hyun Baek, Cole Balintfy, Sarayu Bethamcherla, Shreya Bhargava, Kevin Chang, Sanya Chawla, Emily Chen, Reagan Choi, Shiham Chowdhury, Abhishek Dahad, Raaga Dandavolu, Atharva Dharphale, Malina Dumitrascu, Nikita Ganesh, Rittik Ghosh, Mariska Goswami, Navya Gullapuram, Albert Hua, Nicolas Hung, Jemi Isaac, Neha Jaisankar, Udayvir Jalf, Victoria Jan, Agastya Jayanthi, Sachin Karatha, Hyun Kim, Havesh Kolli, Rishi Konduru, Aileen Liu, Allison Liu, Aditi Locula, Iris Ma, Mlahat Mahmood, Meera Manek, Anay Modi, Brandon Nguyen, Abel Noble, Tanisha Panchal, Esha Patel, Avani Prasad, Ayush Pujara, Vandhana Purushothaman, Yahya Qamar, Eric Qiao, Katie Qu, Danny Samuel, Mohammad Shaik, Navya Shankar, Sanjana Sharma, Rishi Shetty, Heejin Shyn, Kishan Soni, Saakshi Sovani, Sachin Sridhar, Vidhya Harini Srinivas, Smriti Suresh, Dilan Swami, Sharanya Swaminathan, Areej Tahir, Jordan Tansingco, Cole VanAmberg, Rebecca Varghese, Akshay Vasudevan, Andrew Wang, Roger Wang, Claire Wu, Angela Xu, Gary Xu, Rachel Yang and Nancy Yao. The minutes call this a remarkable number of semifinalists and a tribute to the staff and parents of the Troy School District; copies of the resolution were to be presented to the students at a reception on November 3rd.

The resolution recites that student achievement is honored through the National Merit Scholarship semifinalist and finalist recognition programs, and that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). It resolves that the Troy School District Board of Education adopts the resolution in honor of the students for their selection as 2022 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. The vote was Yes 7, No 0, recorded as item 21-081.

Additions & Deletions; Public Communication (Agenda Items)
Both were recorded as None.

General - Consent Agenda, Resolution 21-082
It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B and C on the consent agenda: (A) Minutes of the September 7, 2021 Board of Education Workshop; (B) Minutes of the September 21, 2021 Board of Education Meeting; and (C) Treasurer's Report - August 2021. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Personnel and Curriculum
Both sections were recorded as None.

Business - 2020/2021 Audit Report, Resolution 21-083
Ms. Donna Hanson and Mr. Michael Walsh from Plante Moran provided a presentation to the Board of Education on the audit of the 2020-2021 fiscal year. A draft copy of the District's Audit Report had been presented in detail to the Board at the October 5, 2021 Board Workshop. Ms. Hanson and Mr. Walsh provided highlights of the audit and shared that there were no findings or questioned costs. Governmental funds revenue and expenditures were reviewed, as were student population and foundation allowance. The economic impact of the pandemic challenges, as well as the changes in federal funding, was also discussed at length. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Board of Education accept and approve the Troy School District's audited 2021 financial statements as presented by Plante Moran. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Business - 2021-2022 Amendment of the Operating-All (Hold-Harmless) Millage, Resolution 21-084
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. The resolution recites that the Board, pursuant to a 2021-22 Budget Appropriations Resolution adopted on June 15, 2021, approved the School District's operating, debt and sinking fund millage rates for the 2021-22 school year, which included the authority to levy 4.4575 mills on Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal Properties and 13.5425 mills on all Non-Homestead Properties for a total levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes. It further recites that the FY 22 state school aid act, 2021 PA 48, HB 4411, reduces the amount of hold harmless (OPR ALL) millage districts may levy in 2021 for FY 22; that under section 1211 of the state school code the per pupil hold-harmless revenue is limited to the difference between the district's foundation allowance and $8,700; and that the Board desires to comply with section 1211 of the FY22 state school aid act.

The Board resolved to approve an amendment to the 2021-22 Budget Appropriations Resolution to approve and authorize the School District to modify the Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal and the Non-Homestead Properties millage rate levies for a total levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes. It further resolved to authorize the President and Secretary to sign an amended 2021 Tax Rate Request (Form L-4029) with a Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal Properties millage request of 3.3878, with 1.1591 mills of the 3.3878 to be levied on December 1, 2021, and a Non-Homestead operating millage request of 14.6122, with 7.8409 mills of the 14.6122 mills to be levied on the December 1, 2021 levy date, and that the amended 2021 Tax Rate Request be submitted to the Oakland County Clerk and City of Troy Clerk. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Reports from Student Representatives to the Board
Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East; Sasha Palmkoeck, student representative for Athens High School; and Sarayu Bethamcherla, student representative for Troy High School, each shared a report on events and activities happening in their schools. Alyssa McLarty, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, was not in attendance.

Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items)
President Schmidt shared a statement providing the structure of how the evening's Public Participation would be conducted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines for public comment. Speakers were: Carrie Leser, TSD parent, on a concerning incident occurring at Schroeder Elementary School during morning drop-off and how it is confusing students; Diana Magiera, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask-wearing mandate; Fabrice Smielianskas, TSD parent, in support of the Covid protocols put in place in the district; Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent, on parental rights, displaying pictures from a book found in the school library; Ana Maria Gould, TSD parent, in support of mask-wearing in schools; Yousef Safah, Co-Founder of Mind Matters Education, on mental health support for students; B.J. Lennon, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate; Ashleigh Jennings, TSD parent, in support of the mask mandate; Kacy Bailey, TSD parent, introducing "Moms for Liberty," an Oakland County organization she represents to defend parental rights; Ryan Johnson, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate and expressing concerns of unlawful activities happening; Kelly Jones, TSD parent, in support of the mask mandate; Sarah Krieger, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate; Peggy Chinoski, TSD parent, in support of the mask mandate; and Thomas Fraser, TSD parent, on the recently published Covid Family Guidebook related to quarantine restrictions for students.

Other
Board members congratulated Rick West and his team in the Business Office for the great audit report and their fiscal stewardship, and congratulated the National Merit Semi-Finalists for their accomplishments. Dr. Machesky shared that the Facilities Review Committee (FRC) kicked off its first meeting; the team is comprised of 54 community members and three Board members. He also shared that the Fall Update presentations had begun to building staff and PTOs. Mr. Schmidt shared that the next Board Workshop would be held on Tuesday, November 9th at 6:00 p.m. at the Services Building and the next regular Board Meeting would be Tuesday, November 16th at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

Adjournment
The meeting adjourned at 8:57 p.m.

Minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Troy, Michigan, held November 16, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

Call to Order and Attendance
President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Detmer, Morey and West. There were approximately 85 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:38 p.m.

Recognition - TSD Mission Moment: THS Student Receives Perfect Score on AP Physics Exam
The Board recognized Troy High School senior Reagan Choi for receiving a perfect score on the AP Physics C: Mechanics Exam in May 2021. The minutes note that Reagan's performance was so superior that it fell into an extremely select category; Advanced Placement Exams are college-level examinations scored on a scale of 1 to 5, and Reagan not only received the top score of 5 but is "in the 0.00% in the world for an absolute perfect score." He is one of only two students in the world who answered every single question perfectly. The Board invited teacher Brian Glynn to introduce Reagan and share his accomplishment; Reagan received congratulations from the Board along with a certificate.

Recognition - 2021-22 National Blue Ribbon Awards: Barnard & Leonard Elementary Schools
The Board recognized Barnard Elementary School and Leonard Elementary School for their designation as National Blue-Ribbon Schools, an award honoring them as among the very best schools in the United States. Barnard and Leonard were recognized by U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona at a ceremony in Washington, D.C. on November 4th and 5th. Only 325 schools from around the country were chosen for this honor in 2021. The minutes state the award affirms the hard work of students, staff, parents and the Barnard and Leonard communities, and quote Secretary Cardona: "This year's cohort of honorees demonstrates what is possible when committed educators and school leaders create vibrant, welcoming, and affirming school cultures where rich teaching and learning can flourish," and "I commend our Blue-Ribbon honorees for working to keep students healthy and safe while meeting their academic, social, emotional, and mental health needs. In the face of unprecedented circumstances, you found creative ways to engage, care for, protect, and teach our children. Blue Ribbon Schools have so much to offer and can serve as a model for other schools and communities so that we can truly build back better." The Board invited Melanie Morey, principal of Barnard Elementary School, along with several Barnard staff members, to the podium to say a few words and receive congratulations and a certificate, then invited Dr. Erin Detmer, principal of Leonard Elementary School, along with several Leonard staff members, to do the same.

Additions & Deletions; Public Communication (Agenda Items)
Both recorded as None.

General - Consent Agenda, Resolution 21-085
It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: Minutes of the October 5, 2021 Board of Education Workshop; Minutes of the October 19, 2021 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - September 2021; and Second Reading and Adoption of Board Policies, consisting of revisions to Policy 1000.02 Special Meetings and Policy 2000.06 Student Bullying, and the addition of a policy in Section 8000, Animals on District Property. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Personnel, Resolution 21-086
It was moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Dr. Wilson that the Board of Education approve the personnel recommendations as stated, identified in the minutes as New Hires: Aaron Ducharme and Toby Klein. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Curriculum
Recorded as None.

Business - Bus Purchase, Resolution 21-087
It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $931,182.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2013 Bond Series 3. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Business - CAD Lab Computers, Resolution 21-088
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for CAD Lab Computers be awarded to Sehi Computer Products in the amount of $66,096 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and General Fund. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Reports from Student Representatives to the Board
Sasha Palmkoeck, student representative for Athens High School; Sarayu Bethamcherla, student representative for Troy High School; Alyssa McLarty, student representative for Troy College and Career High School; and Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, each shared a report on the events and activities happening in their schools.

Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items)
President Schmidt shared a statement providing the structure of how the evening's Public Participation would be conducted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines to be followed for public comment. Speakers were:

- Mrs. Kristina Gerami, TSD parent, on concerns about prejudice in the Troy School District and the struggles her child has had in school.
- Mrs. Katie MacFarland, TSD parent, on her dissatisfaction with how the book review of Fun Home was handled, and concerns about another book reviewed in 2015, What My Mother Doesn't Know, that is now available at Baker Middle School.
- Ms. Rebecca Han, TSD community member, on concerns with the District's summer reading AP English class and the suggested reading materials offered.
- Ms. Barbara Yagley, TSD community member, with concerns about graphic novels as grooming tools, stating that pedophiles have used these and that the Board are guardians who should not let that creep into the schools.
- Mrs. Diana Magiera, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate, stating that leadership does not respect parents and describing the hostile environment it has created.
- B.J. Lennon, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate in place in the Troy School District.
- Ryan Johnson, TSD parent, on diversity and equity and CRT and his opposition to the mask mandate; he demanded the immediate resignation of the superintendent and all Board members and threatened to sue each person for what he considers breaking the law, including the mask mandate, and unenrolling his son from school.
- Mr. Joe Thilman, Troy community member, in support of the mask mandate, thanking the Board for promoting concern for others and urging it to continue doing the right thing by working together.
- Stephanie Margilaj, TSD parent, on DEI and "the real crisis in the school system," discussing her concerns with the transformation of public education.
- Mr. Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent, on parental rights, displaying graphic pictures from a book found in the school library and discussing the book review committee.
- Heidi Fentress, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate and also raising that her student was not able to use the bathrooms at Troy High during the day because they were closed.
- Sarah Krieger, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate in the Troy School District.
- Mrs. Nahla Hassan, TSD parent, on special education services for her high school student and how children with disabilities have a right to FAPE.
- Mr. John Tyson, TSD community member, on focusing on education and not indoctrination.
- Mr. Daniel Kang, Athens High School graduate, on initiating a plan to change computer science classes to allow for more programming courses.

Other
Recorded as None.

Board Member Comments
Dr. Philippart shared that she attended the MASB conference the previous week and gave kudos to Karl Schmidt and Dr. Wilson for their work presenting the TSD Board Self-Evaluation tool, built off Michael Fullan's work. Mrs. Hammond shared that she attended the Troy College and Career High School PTO meeting and commented on how nice the building was. Mr. Gottlieb commented on Troy's participation in the NPDL Global Learning program and the great work being done with students. Mrs. Anne also commented on how insightful and useful the MASB Conference was. Mr. Hauff wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving and shared how grateful he is for the Board and Central Office administration. Dr. Wilson shared that she attended the Troy High play Pride & Prejudice and is excited to see Elf performed by the Athens Theatre Ensemble. Dr. Machesky indicated he is almost finished presenting the TSD Fall Update to staff and PTOs, sharing the challenges the District faces, and thanked the Board for their hard work and continued daily support. Mr. Schmidt shared that he and Dr. Wilson spent a half-day at the preschool for Trunk or Treat and mentioned how well everything functions at full capacity. He announced that the next Board Workshop would be held on Tuesday, December 7th at 6:00 p.m. at the Services Building and the next regular Board Meeting would be Tuesday, December 14th at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

Adjournment
The meeting adjourned at 8:38 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education's combined annual organizational and regular meeting held remotely via Zoom Webinar on January 19, 2021, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:06 p.m. and adjourned at 9:22 p.m. with roughly 275 additional audience members present. The Board re-elected Schmidt president (6-1, Hammond opposed), Wilson vice president, Hauff secretary, and appointed Rick L. West treasurer, then adopted resolutions on fund depositories, legal counsel, meeting schedule and committee assignments. On a 5-2 vote it authorized the Superintendent to amend the Robertson Brothers Co. purchase agreement for the Square Lake Road surplus land sold for $1,425,000.00.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education, Troy, Michigan. Board meeting minutes for January 19, 2021, held remotely via Zoom Webinar after public notice permitting remote community participation. Called to order by President Schmidt at 7:06 p.m.; adjourned at 9:22 p.m. Minutes signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (GNH/jh).

**Attendance**
Board members present by Zoom videoconference from locations in Troy, Michigan: Schmidt, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present: Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Moynihan, Carson, Zawislak, Harris and West; Dana Abrahams of Clark Hill, P.C.; two Student Board Reps; approximately 275 additional audience members.

**Student representatives**
Nathania Nartey (Athens High School) and Pranay Gupta (International Academy-East) reported. Sejal Patil (Troy High School) and Carlton Thomas (Troy College & Career High School) were not in attendance.

**Organizational actions**

| Item | Action | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 21-002 | Schmidt as acting chairperson (Philippart/Wilson) | 7-0 |
| -- | Judy Holmes appointed temporary secretary | -- |
| 21-003 | Schmidt president through December 31, 2021 (Hauff/Anne) | 6 yes; 1 no (Hammond) |
| 21-004 | Wilson vice president through December 31, 2021 (Philippart/Anne) | 7-0 |
| 21-005 | Hauff secretary through December 31, 2021 (Hammond/Philippart) | 7-0 |
| 21-006 | Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent Business Services, appointed Treasurer January-December 2021 (Philippart/Anne) | 7-0 |
| 21-007 | Fund Depositories and Investments resolution (Philippart/Hammond) | 7-0 |
| 21-008 | Legal counsel designations for calendar 2021 (Anne/Philippart) | 7-0 |
| 21-009 | Superintendent designated Deputy Secretary for 2021 (Hammond/Hauff) | 7-0 |
| 21-010 | Judy Holmes designated to post meeting notices for 2021 (Wilson/Hauff) | 7-0 |
| 21-011 | 2021 calendar-year meeting schedule (Anne/Philippart) | 7-0 |
| 21-012 | 2021 Board Committee Memberships (Hauff/Philippart) | 7-0 |

**Depositories**
Bank of America, Charter One Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and PNC Bank. Investments follow Board Policy 5000.06 and Section 380.1223(1)(h) of the Revised School Code.

**Recognition**
Mission Moment honoring six LERN (Leading for Equity Design Network) student teammates, part of the National Equity Project; presented by Assistant Superintendent DiPilato and Troy High Assistant Principal Brian Zawislak. January is School Board Appreciation Month; trustees received a long-sleeved oneTROY pullover.

**Public communication**
Tony Lucchi (TEA President), Jason Cichowicz (TEA representative, 5th grade teacher at Schroeder Elementary) and Jeff Rainwater (teacher, Troy College and Career High School) addressed the Board on the safety and timing of returning teachers and students to buildings.

**Business and other actions**
21-013 consent agenda items A through G approved 7-0. 21-014 roof replacement bid awarded from Capital Projects & Building Site Sinking Funds, 7-0. 21-015 Site Work Paving Program bid awarded from the same funds, 7-0. 21-016 authorization to amend the Section 1 purchase agreement with Robertson Brothers Co. passed 5-2 (Gottlieb and Hammond opposed). 21-017 reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan passed 6-1 (Hammond opposed).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Convening.** The Troy Board of Education met on January 19, 2021 remotely via Zoom Webinar, with public notice posted so community members could participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:06 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson were present via Zoom videoconference, each connecting from Troy, Michigan and each stating name and location for the roll. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Moynihan, Carson, Zawislak, Harris and West; Dana Abrahams from Clark Hill, P.C.; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 275 additional members of the audience. Mr. Schmidt explained that this meeting is where the Board elects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year and approves or authorizes items considered on an annual basis, with the regular Board meeting following the organizational portion.

**Student representatives.** Because student representatives needed to prepare for mid-terms, they reported first. Nathania Nartey, Student Representative for Athens High School, and Pranay Gupta, Student Representative for the International Academy-East, shared updates. Sejal Patil, Student Representative for Troy High School, and Carlton Thomas, Student Representative for Troy College & Career High School, were not in attendance.

**Officer elections.** Resolution 21-002: moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson that Mr. Schmidt serve as acting chairperson until election of a president; roll call 7 yes, 0 no. Mr. Schmidt then appointed Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until election of the Board secretary. Resolution 21-003: Mr. Hauff nominated Mr. Schmidt for president; nominations closed on a motion by Dr. Wilson supported by Dr. Philippart, 7 yes, 0 no; the resolution that Mr. Schmidt serve as president until December 31, 2021 was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne and carried 6 yes (Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb) to 1 no (Hammond). Resolution 21-004: Dr. Philippart nominated Dr. Wilson for vice president; nominations closed 7 yes, 0 no; the resolution that Dr. Wilson serve as vice president until December 31, 2021 was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne, carrying 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-005: Mrs. Hammond nominated Mr. Hauff for secretary; nominations closed 7 yes, 0 no; the resolution that Mr. Hauff serve as secretary until December 31, 2021 was moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Dr. Philippart, carrying 7 yes, 0 no.

**Treasurer.** Resolution 21-006, moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne, appointed Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, as Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for the period January through December 2021. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Fund depositories and investments.** Resolution 21-007, moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Hammond, adopted the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for January through December 2021 and directed that the attached resolution be incorporated in its entirety into the official minutes. The resolution recites that public monies, including tax monies, coming into the hands of Rick West, Treasurer of Troy School District, are to be deposited or invested in his name as Treasurer with the following institutions: Bank of America, Charter One Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks signed with the facsimile signature of Treasurer Rick West, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of Rick West or of Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be drawn on by checks with the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The account established at Comerica Bank for paying health care and dependent care flexible spending claims may be drawn by ACH debit to Next Generation Enrollment, Inc. or by checks with the Treasurer's facsimile signature. The Treasurer may open or close accounts with the listed institutions when in the District's interest; funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06; and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund for an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code, with the maximum amount to be invested regulated by the school code. The certification is signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, given under hand and seal this 19th day of January 2021. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Legal counsel.** Resolution 21-008, moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart, continued the designation of Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; Beier Howlett, P.C.; and Miller Canfield P.L.C. as legal counsel to advise or represent the Troy School District and Board of Education as necessary for the 2021 calendar year, with the Superintendent authorized to consult additional counsel as needed with prior notification to the Board. Mr. Gottlieb stated that he feels it is critical to have dialogue and discourse with the various law firms the district engages. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Other annual designations.** Resolution 21-009, moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Hauff, continued the designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board with authority to act for the secretary for calendar 2021; 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-010, moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff, designated Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools, as the person for posting notices of meetings for 2021; 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-011, moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart, adopted the schedule of meetings for the 2021 calendar year as shown on the attached calendar; 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-012, moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Philippart, adopted the Board Committee Memberships for the 2021 school year as attached; 7 yes, 0 no.

**Recognition: LERN Network student teammates.** As the evening's Mission Moment the Board recognized six students serving on the LERN Network. Mrs. DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, explained that LERN is the Leading for Equity Design Network, part of the National Equity Project (NEP) with which the Troy School District has been working, and that the team is made up of faculty, teachers, administrators and student representatives. She introduced Troy High School Assistant Principal Brian Zawislak, the team's student liaison, who noted the six student leaders joined LERN in December and introduced Sarayu Bethamcharla (Troy High), Kian Schneeweis (Baker Middle School), Gianna Pearson (Athens High School) and Wamucie Karimi (Troy High). Noah Veen (Troy College & Career High School) and Erik Schmidt (Athens) are also LERN student representatives but were unable to attend. Students described wanting to lift the power of student voice around diversity, inclusion and equity; one student shared a challenge experienced in school and how he overcame it.

**Board Recognition Month.** Each January the Troy School District honors the trustees of its Board of Education. School Board Appreciation Month recognizes the role trustees play in reinforcing the mission of the Troy School District, ensuring learning for all, through policies, fiscal stewardship and support of teaching and learning. As a symbol of appreciation the District presented each trustee a long-sleeved oneTROY pullover.

**Additions and deletions; public communication.** There were no additions or deletions. Under public communication on non-agenda items, Tony Lucchi, President of the Troy Education Association (TEA), addressed the Board about having teachers return to buildings for in-seat and hybrid instruction during the pandemic, discussing safety issues and the need for teachers to be vaccinated before returning. Jason Cichowicz, TEA representative and 5th grade teacher at Schroeder Elementary, addressed the safety of returning teachers and students and the inequity of elementary schedules compared to secondary. Jeff Rainwater, teacher at Troy College and Career High School, addressed returning to in-seat instruction too soon and how having COVID in the fall affected him and his family. A later public communication period drew no speakers.

**Consent agenda.** Resolution 21-013, moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond, approved items A through G: corrections to the November Workshop and Meeting Minutes to include the location where Board members participated remotely; minutes of the December 1, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 15, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 18, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 18, 2020 Closed Session Meeting; Treasurer's Report for November 2020; and appointment of the Board Negotiating Team for TEA Contract Negotiations. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Business items.** Resolution 21-014 (Roofing), moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff, awarded the bid roof replacement and approved the amount as an expenditure of the Capital Projects & Building Site Sinking Funds; roll call 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-015 (Site Work - Paving), moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart, awarded the bid Site Work Paving Program and approved the amount as an expenditure of the Capital Projects & Building Site Sinking Funds; roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Section 1 Purchase Agreement Amendment.** Resolution 21-016 was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff. It recites that the School District passed a resolution on April 21, 2020 authorizing the sale of surplus real property in the City of Troy, Oakland County, Michigan, described as 6.12 +/- acres of vacant land located on the North side of Square Lake Road, East of John R Road, the Premises being part of a larger 70.647 +/- acre parcel (Parcel 2), with the District additionally including an 11.281 +/- acre parcel (Parcel 1); the undeveloped portion of Parcel 2 and all of Parcel 1 are to remain preserved in perpetuity through a conservation easement. In compliance with that resolution the Superintendent negotiated and executed an offer to purchase dated June 8, 2020 with Robertson Brothers Co., on behalf of an entity to be formed, to purchase the Premises for One Million Four Hundred Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($1,425,000.00) Dollars with an earnest money deposit of Fifty Thousand and 00/100 ($50,000.00) Dollars. The District and Purchaser then learned that up to an additional 6.29 acres of land must be deeded to the Purchaser to obtain the density bonus assumed in the Purchaser's Concept Plan under the City's One-Family Cluster Option Ordinance, which Concept Plan was incorporated by reference into the Purchase Agreement. The amendment would deed the additional acreage at Closing while making clear the additional acreage remains preserved as open space in perpetuity except for the storm pond/basin, the trailhead gravel parking lot and other similar requirements necessary for the proposed development. The resolution authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to negotiate the amendment, adjust Purchase Agreement timelines, and execute the amendment and all documents incidental to the sale after consultation with legal counsel. Board members, administration and attorney Dana Abrahams discussed the topic. Roll call: 5 yes (Anne, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson), 2 no (Gottlieb, Hammond).

**COVID-19 plan reconfirmation.** Under Other, the Extended Learning Plan was listed. Dr. Machesky shared information about the most recent COVID case numbers in Michigan and Oakland County, encouraged the community to visit the District's website for updated COVID data, and stated that no changes were being recommended at that time to the Return to Learn Plan. Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure for schools planning a return of Pre-K through Post High School education, requiring Michigan districts to adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan addressing the phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan, to submit a reconfirmation plan to the Board monthly, and to post the Preparedness Plan on the district website home page. Resolution 21-017, moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff, approved the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan; roll call 6 yes (Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb), 1 no (Hammond).

**Adjournment.** The meeting was adjourned at 9:22 p.m. Minutes respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the notation GNH/jh.

**Publication**
Pages from the MASB candidate booklet for the 2021 elections, running from page 22 ("Candidates for MASB Board of Directors") through page 25 ("2021 Elections"). All four profiles are for Region 8, Three-Year Term.

**Candidate roster**

| Candidate | District / County | Time served | Offices held | MASB certification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sandra Dukhie | Ferndale Public Schools, Oakland County | Four years | Vice President | (listed without award entries) |
