It catalogs each discipline's current responsibilities across consultation, evaluation, crisis response and MTSS Tiers 1 through 3, describes Student Assistance Team membership and SRSS screening completed four times per year at secondary and three times per year at elementary, and presents a November staff module on anxiety citing that 7.1% of children (4.4 million) ages 3-17 have a diagnosed anxiety disorder and that 80% of children who have anxiety do not get help.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What it is**
Presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education titled "Mental Health Supports - School Counselors, Psychologists and Social Work: creating a system of support for students and the school community," describing the current roles of each of the three support disciplines, the district's tiered structures, and a sample staff professional development module on anxiety.

**School counselors - current state**
Consultation and therapeutic intervention duties include individual therapeutic intervention; crisis intervention at the individual, familial and building level; threat assessment for suicidal ideation; the referral process; coordination with in-patient and out-patient therapists; social emotional support during disciplinary hearings; 9th grade interactive SEL classes; therapy dogs; restorative practices; At-Risk/SRSS/SEL/MTSS work; participation in SST; and teacher and staff mental wellbeing support. Events include 9-12 class meetings, 8th grade student and parent presentations, junior college-planning and testing presentations, College Night, Honors Convocation, graduation, college visits and a financial aid evening. Caseload duties include college planning meetings with every senior, individual scheduling for every student, two weeks of schedule changes at each semester start, enrollment and placement testing, AP test coordination, Common Application letters of recommendation, National Merit Semi-Finalist and Presidential Scholars applications, OSTC, 504 referrals, IEP annual meetings, 21F, NCAA, virtual at-home and foreign exchange students, scholarships, newsletter, military, Weebly/Twitter/Instagram, and the Seal of Bi-Literacy.

**School psychologists - current state**
Support struggling and diverse learners, academic achievement, positive behavior and mental health, safe learning environments, school-family-community partnerships and school-wide data-based decision making. Duties span consultation, REED and evaluation (CA-60 review, classroom consult, data analysis, REED and Prior Written Notice development, formal assessments, facilitating initial MET/IEP meetings) and pre-referral work across Tier 1 (needs assessment, benchmarking, SRSS data mining, SEL training, PBIS), Tier 2 (short-term direct intervention, systematic observation, progress data, P2P) and Tier 3 (executive coaching, Functional Behavior Assessments and PBIS plans, staff training). They also maintain CPI certification and serve on the building Key Identified Personnel (KIP) team.

**School social workers - current state**
Carry IEP or Section 504 caseloads, conduct eligibility evaluations, maintain service records and progress monitoring, handle Medicaid documentation and billing, lead Functional Behavior Assessments and Positive Behavioral Intervention Support Plans, train HCA/staff, monitor discipline and facilitate MDR, serve as KIP leader, and connect families to community resources. Tiered work runs from schoolwide SEL training, Zones of Regulation and bi-weekly principal meetings on SEL data, through Tier 2 check-in/check-out and four to six week small-group or 1:1 instruction, to Tier 3 eight to twelve week intensive instruction and crisis response including CPS referral.

**Structures**
Student Assistance Teams at elementary include the teacher consultant, school psychologist, school social worker, speech language pathologist, ELD, literacy specialist, math interventionist, principal and general education teacher; secondary teams include the school psychologist, school social worker, speech and language pathologist, special education teachers, counselors, assistant principal and principal. The SRSS screener is completed four times per year at secondary (at semester) and three times per year at elementary, providing one piece of data for building teams.

**Staff capacity building - anxiety module (November SEL series)**
Cited statistics: 7.1% of children (4.4 million) ages 3-17 have a diagnosed anxiety disorder; 32% of adolescents are estimated to have anxiety in the United States; 80% of children who have anxiety do not get help; higher levels are seen in females; among children diagnosed with anxiety, 1 in 3 will have a behavioral problem, and among children with behavior issues, 1 in 3 will be anxious. Sources include the American Psychological Association, NIMH, CDC and Jessica Minahan.

**Next steps**
Continue developing district and building structures, establish community partnerships, build capacity and understanding around mental health, strengthen connections for students, enhance social emotional learning in all buildings, develop crisis response training, and continue identifying needs in Tiers 1, 2 and 3.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board presentation titled "Mental Health Supports - School Counselors, Psychologists and Social Work: creating a system of support for students and the school community," delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on February 1, 2022. It inventories the current responsibilities of each of the three student-support disciplines, describes the district's tiered systems and team structures, presents a sample staff professional development module on anxiety, and lists next steps.

SCHOOL COUNSELORS - CURRENT STATE. Under consultation and therapeutic intervention, counselors provide individual therapeutic intervention; crisis intervention at the individual, familial and building level; threat assessment for suicidal ideation; the referral process; coordination and communication with in-patient and out-patient therapists; collaboration with administration; social emotional support during disciplinary hearings; 9th grade interactive SEL classes; therapy dogs; restorative practices with administration; At-Risk, SRSS, SEL and MTSS work with all students; participation in SST; staff meeting presentations on SEL support and crisis intervention support; and teacher and staff mental wellbeing support. Under events and presentations, counselors run 9, 10, 11 and 12 grade class meetings; 8th grade student presentations and meetings at all middle schools; an 8th grade parent evening presentation with Q&A; junior presentations for college planning and standardized testing; College Night; the Honors Convocation evening event; graduation; college visits; and a financial aid evening event. Caseload responsibilities include management of an individual caseload; an individual college planning meeting with every senior student; individual scheduling for every student; schedule changes for two weeks at the start of semester 1 and semester 2; enrollment of new students and placement testing; AP test coordination; college applications including the Common Application with letters of recommendation for all seniors; National Merit Semi-Finalist applications; Presidential Scholars applications; OSTC; 504 referrals and management of all 504s at the middle school level; IEP annual meetings; 21F; NCAA; virtual at-home students; foreign exchange students; scholarships; the newsletter; military; website and social media via Weebly, Twitter and Instagram; and the Seal of Bi-Literacy.

SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGISTS - CURRENT STATE. School psychologists support struggling and diverse learners, academic achievement, positive behavior and mental health, safe and supportive learning environments, school-family-community partnerships, and school-wide data-based decision making. Their consultation, REED and evaluation work includes collaborating with local district administrators and school-based leadership teams on MTSS activities, participating in problem-solving teams requiring knowledge of data collection and analysis, curriculum-based assessments and tiered systems of interventions; comprehensive review of the CA-60; general education classroom consultation; data collection and analysis; supporting staff in identifying and using research-based instructional practices; attending grade level and special education data review meetings and secondary department meetings; working with the building principal and/or interventionist or department leads to select a grade level or department to support; REED and Prior Written Notice (PWN) development; formal assessments as directed by the REED; and scheduling initial IEPs, creating the initial invitation and facilitating MET/IEP meetings. Pre-referral duties are organized in tiers. At Tier 1 psychologists may perform a building needs assessment, assist in benchmarking to establish baseline data for at-risk students, help mine SRSS data and take an active role in problem solving, provide consultation and support for Tier 1 at-risk classes and students at the secondary level, deliver SEL training for all staff, and support classroom and building implementation of universal supports and PBIS. At Tier 2 they provide short-term direct intervention in areas of identified need, recommend classroom interventions for at-risk students, collect data during systematic observations, maintain current performance data documenting progress and intervention effectiveness with re-evaluation as needed, may assist with a P2P partner, and may be assigned as an intervention partner to determine next steps. At Tier 3 they may function as an executive coach, assist with Functional Behavior Assessments and PBIS plan development, assist with training teachers, teams and support staff in Tier 3 interventions, collaborate with the behavior support team, and conduct follow-up observations and meetings. Additional responsibilities include providing professional learning and consultative services to local educational staff upon request, establishing and attending departmental professional learning, case study collaboration, maintaining CPI certification, participating on the building Key Identified Personnel (KIP) team, building capacity and consistency in school psychologists' practices, and sensitivity training for student-specific needs.

SCHOOL SOCIAL WORKERS - CURRENT STATE. Social workers carry an IEP or Section 504 caseload and are active MTSS participants and team members. Duties include providing direct or consultative services through needs identified in the IEP or 504 process; collaborating on IEP development; conducting evaluations to determine or re-determine eligibility and service needs; maintaining service records and progress monitoring; Medicaid documentation and billing; serving as team leader for Functional Behavior Assessments and Positive Behavioral Intervention Support Plans; collaborating with outside therapists and support services; providing community resources and direct support to families; training HCAs and staff on PBIS plan implementation; monitoring discipline and facilitating MDR; serving as Key Identified Personnel (KIP) leader; sensitivity training for student-specific needs; and working with general education teachers on student needs and interventions. Tier 1 schoolwide work includes serving as KIP team member and leader for all students, building team member for student, staff and family crisis and trauma intervention, attending SSW discipline meetings and building meetings to collaborate on SEL, attending special education department meetings, collaborating with families and outside therapists or agencies, providing community resources, leading professional development on tiered socio-emotional and behavioral supports, scheduling bi-weekly meetings with the building principal to review schoolwide and student-specific SEL data, supporting any student in immediate crisis or danger such as through the safety protocol for suicide or self-injurious behavior, facilitating and educating on CPS referral, delivering SEL training for all staff, supporting universal supports implementation, reviewing SRSS data, collaborating on the school improvement team including PBIS implementation, implementing Zones of Regulation, and push-in whole group lessons one to three times. Tier 2 work includes collaborating with general education teachers interested in P2P, working on classroom-wide PBIS systems, joining grade level meetings when SEL data is discussed, leading development of Tier 2 PBIS plans such as check-in/check-out and token systems, Zones of Regulation Tier 2 support, serving as a P2P partner, identifying data collection systems, targeted push-in whole group short-term general education lessons such as executive functioning, short-term four to six week small-group or 1:1 instruction with skill-specific data collection, and observation and follow-up to determine next steps. Tier 3 work includes Zones of Regulation Tier 3 support, check-ins for students who identify as being in the "red zone" during daily reporting, team leadership for Functional Behavior Assessments and PBIS plan development, Peer to Peer leadership, training teachers, teams and support staff in Tier 3 interventions, collaboration with the behavior support team, longer-term eight to twelve week intensive small-group or 1:1 instruction, parent communication, and follow-up observation and meetings.

UNIQUE SKILLS. School counselors are distinguished by individualized therapeutic intervention, secondary and post-secondary academic counseling and planning, standardized testing coordination, large group developmental interventions, threat assessment, and vocational and career development. School psychologists focus on child development from birth through 26 years of age, individual behavior, academic and ability assessment, and consultation, data analysis and problem solving at the systems, building, classroom and individual level. School social workers focus on identification of students at risk, early intervention, problem solving services to students, parent interactions, school personnel, behavioral intervention and student crisis response, and involvement with community agencies.

TEAM STRUCTURES AND SCREENING. Elementary Student Assistance Team members are the teacher consultant, school psychologist, school social worker, speech language pathologist, ELD, literacy specialist, math interventionist, principal and general education teacher. Secondary team members are the school psychologist, school social worker, speech and language pathologist, special education teachers, counselors, assistant principal and principal. Secondary buildings complete the SRSS screener four times per year, at semester, and elementary buildings complete it three times per year; SRSS provides one piece of data for building teams to review when determining student social-emotional needs. Staff capacity is built through monthly presentations on topics intended to simultaneously build understanding and capacity across the district.

ANXIETY MODULE (SEL PRESENTATION SERIES, NOVEMBER). The sample module reports that 7.1% of children (4.4 million) ages 3-17 have a diagnosed anxiety disorder, that 32% of adolescents are estimated to have anxiety in the United States, that 80% of children who have anxiety do not get help, that higher levels of anxiety are seen in females, that among children diagnosed with anxiety 1 in 3 will have a behavioral problem, and that among children who have issues with behavior 1 in 3 will be anxious. Signs in the school setting include difficulty concentrating, distraction, forgetfulness, difficulty shifting attention between tasks, inattentiveness, negative behavior change, changed peer or adult relationships, poor academic performance, difficulty initiating tasks, appearing unmotivated, lazy or uninterested, perfectionism, school avoidance or refusal, social withdrawal, increased complaining, clinginess, negative thoughts, fear of failure or embarrassment, and rigid or inflexible thinking. Anxiety is described as impairing intake of new information and long-term memory, executive functioning such as planning and working memory, social interactions including group work and presenting, perspective-taking and transitions, and as creating all-or-nothing thinking. Teacher guidance under "Put Your Oxygen Mask on First" covers setting literal or metaphorical boundaries, self-validation, expanding one's social support "village" because social support increases resilience, self-care beyond bubble baths, and modeling non-anxious coping by tolerating uncertainty, focusing on the here and now and being genuine. Listed resources include anxietyintheclassroom.org, a School Resources Wakelet, gozen.com, the MGH PRIDE learning management course, a Feeling Thermometer by Aureen Wagner, PhD, and mindfulschools.org. Sources cited are the American Psychological Association, the National Institute of Mental Health, the CDC's children's mental health data pages, anxietyintheclassroom.org and Jessica Minahan.

NEXT STEPS. Continue to develop structures at the district and building levels; establish community partnerships; continue to build capacity and understanding around mental health; strengthen connections for students; enhance social emotional learning in all buildings; develop crisis response training; and continue to identify needs in Tiers 1, 2 and 3.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC issued this draft Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District on October 5, 2021, communicating results of its audit of the district's financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2021 plus informational items on Michigan school finance. The auditors report no disagreements with management, no significant difficulties, and no new accounting policies, and identify the district's share of MPSERS net liabilities, estimated at $308,094,061 for pension and $48,088,931 for OPEB, as the most sensitive estimates. General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, lifting fund balance to approximately $32,700,000, or 19.88 percent of expenditures.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Document.** Draft "Report to the Board of Education," Troy School District, June 30, 2021, prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC and dated October 5, 2021. Signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Manager). Organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-6) and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office for their assistance.

**Audit scope and communications.** The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; planning matters were discussed with the board on August 13, 2021. The audit was conducted under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards, with a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 on internal control over financial reporting and compliance. A federal program audit under 2 CFR Part 200 was also completed, reported separately on October 5, 2021. Management representations are contained in a letter dated October 5, 2021.

**Significant audit findings.** No new accounting policies were adopted and no existing policies changed during 2021. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance; none were recorded in a different period than they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the district's shares of the MPSERS net pension and OPEB liabilities under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, estimated at $308,094,061 and $48,088,931 respectively as of June 30, 2021, based on Office of Retirement Services data. Disclosures were judged neutral, consistent, and clear. Management corrected all identified immaterial misstatements. There were no disagreements with management and no difficulties in performing the audit.

**State aid background.** The May 2020 Revenue Estimating Conference suggested proration of roughly $685 per pupil; by the August 2020 conference the actual proration for 2019-2020 was $175 per pupil. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at 2019-2020 levels, with a target foundation of $8,529, a minimum of $8,111, and a one-time $65 per pupil payment not folded into the formula. A one-year "super blend" pupil count weighted the 2019-2020 count at 75 percent and the 2020-2021 count at 25 percent. For 2021-2022 the target foundation rises to $8,700 per pupil, with a $171 per pupil increase for districts already at or above target; for hold harmless districts such as Troy the increase is expected as $115 of foundation allowance plus $56 of Section 20m funding. Counts return to 90 percent fall / 10 percent spring weighting.

**Retirement and federal relief figures.**

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Section 147a1 | $1,070,809 |
| Section 147a2 | $1,838,621 |
| Section 147c1 | $11,658,202 |
| Section 147e | $206,687 |
| Coronavirus Relief Fund available | $4,588,959 |
| ESSER I award | $246,411 |
| ESSER II estimate | $843,258 |
| ESSER III estimate | $1,893,840 |
| ESSER II state equalization payment | $5,036,199 |

The 2020-2021 MPSERS contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, and from 20.96 to 28.21 percent net of state support; total contributions represent about 42 percent of covered payroll with roughly 28 percent borne net by the district. For 2022 the overall rate is expected to rise to 43 percent from 42 percent with the net share near 28 percent. CRF distributions were approximately $362 per pupil; the award was fully expended in fiscal 2021. The ESSER II funding floor was $450 per pupil and the ESSER III floor $1,093 per student, the latter now questioned by the federal government.

**MPSERS plan status.** At September 30, 2020 the plan's net pension liability was approximately $35 billion, up from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, an increase of about 3.5 percent. The net OPEB liability was approximately $5.4 billion, down from $7.3 billion, a decrease of about 26 percent, reflecting a health care cost trend rate reduction from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable plan experience.

**Fund balance.** General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000 in 2020-2021, increasing General Fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, equal to about eight weeks of operations; Troy's percentage is 19.88 percent, about 10.3 weeks.

**Forward-looking items.** Recommendations cover grants management risk assessment, budgeting for nonrecurring federal aid with program end dates laddered through 2024, cybersecurity (the "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act" introduced in the House in June 2021 would appropriate $10M yearly for two years), IT assessment, GASB Statement No. 87 on leases effective for the June 30, 2022 statements, SAS No. 134 changing the auditor's report for June 30, 2022, and the GASB financial reporting model exposure draft with phased adoption at June 30, 2025 for districts with revenue over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under. The next Revenue Estimating Conference is set for January 2022.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Plante & Moran, PLLC prepared this draft "Report to the Board of Education" for Troy School District covering the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021. The transmittal letter and each substantive letter within it are dated October 5, 2021. The report is divided into Results of the Audit (pages 1-6) and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The firm extends thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to normal daily activities. The letter is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Manager.

**Responsibility and scope.** As stated in the engagement letter dated June 2, 2021, the auditor's responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with board oversight are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement and does not relieve the board or management of their responsibilities. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the firm must communicate matters involving compliance with laws, regulations, contracts and grant agreements, instances of error or fraud, illegal acts applicable to government agencies, and significant deficiencies in internal control; a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 was issued on internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance. The audit followed the planned scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of August 13, 2021.

**Significant audit findings.** Management is responsible for the selection and use of accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2021. No transactions were entered into for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions were recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive accounting estimates were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. As of June 30, 2021 those estimates were $308,094,061 for pension and $48,088,931 for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, management corrected all immaterial misstatements identified, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. A federal program audit required by 2 CFR Part 200 was completed, with results reported separately on October 5, 2021. Management representations are included in a letter dated October 5, 2021. The firm read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and found nothing materially inconsistent with the financial statements. The information is intended solely for the Board of Education and management.

**Informational items - state aid background.** The report frames the period as "A Year Like No Other" and traces the move "From 18 Months of Financial Uncertainty to Projected Stability." Before the pandemic, state resources were stable and predictable. In spring 2020 substantial proration of state aid was feared, prompting two Revenue Estimating Conferences, the scheduled May 2020 conference and an additional August 2020 conference. The May conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil, and many districts adopted final 2020 budget amendments on that basis; by August 2020 the actual proration for the 2019-2020 fiscal year was set at $175 per pupil. Beginning in March 2020 the federal government provided several waves of assistance with evolving spending requirements, though COVID-19 relief funds ultimately allowed more flexibility than traditional federal grants. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at the 2019-2020 level, no prorations were required, and a $65 one-time per pupil payment was provided; the State also supplemented districts that did not reach a minimum per pupil threshold from the Educational Stabilization Fund. For 2021-2022 all schools move to a target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap between base and target, and all districts including hold harmless districts receive at least a $171 per pupil increase, with added funding for special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and the Great Start Readiness Program (GSRP), reflecting School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations.

**2021 funding implications for Troy.** Because of pandemic-related concerns, 2020-2021 foundation levels were maintained at 2019-2020 levels: the target foundation allowance (formerly the basic foundation allowance) was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111, with the one-time $65 per pupil payment excluded from the formula and not retained for 2021-2022. For 2020-2021 a one-year "super blend" pupil count combined the 2019-2020 count weighted at 75 percent with the 2020-2021 count weighted at 25 percent, multiplied by the foundation allowance per pupil to determine total foundation funding.

**MPSERS cost support.** Contributions are computed as a percentage of payroll and the required rate continues to increase. The estimated 2020-2021 contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, and the rate net of state funding support paid directly by the employer ranged from 20.96 to 28.21 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act. Troy received $1,070,809 in 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 of 147e. Total retirement contributions represent approximately 42 percent of covered payroll recognized as expenditure, with the district responsible for approximately a 28 percent net contribution.

**Coronavirus Relief Fund and other federal funding.** In summer 2020 approximately $362 per pupil was provided to districts by the Michigan Department of Education through summer state aid payments; the total available to Troy was $4,588,959. Because the funding was not approved until July 2020, revenue recognition was deferred to fiscal year 2021, and for the year ended June 30, 2021 the district fully expended the award and recognized the related federal revenue. Two key funding sources are the Education Stabilization Fund (ESF), whose principal programs are the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) Fund and the Governor's Education Emergency Relief (GEER) Fund, and the Coronavirus Relief Fund (CRF), which includes the $362 per pupil passed through by MDE plus amounts from other nonfederal entities. Reimbursement claims could reach back to costs incurred as early as March 2020.

**ESSER awards.** ESSER grants come in three waves: ESSER I, ESSER II (divided between phase 1 and phase 2), and ESSER III. The district's ESSER I award was $246,411; ESSER II and III estimates are $843,258 and $1,893,840 respectively. ESSER I revenue could be recognized in fiscal 2021 to the extent allowable expenditures were incurred. Phase 1 ESSER II revenue could be recognized in fiscal 2021 only if a grant award letter was received by June 30, 2021; many districts did not receive theirs, deferring recognition to fiscal 2022. Phase 2 of ESSER II and ESSER III awards become available in fiscal 2022. ESSER allocations use the Title I model based on economically disadvantaged demographics, so the Legislature and governor established a floor of $450 per pupil for ESSER II with state equalization payments. Based on its ESSER II level, Troy qualified for an equalization payment of $5,036,199, received over the May through August 2021 state aid payments; the district recognized a portion as fiscal 2021 revenue and will recognize the remainder in fiscal 2022. For ESSER III the state set a funding floor of $1,093 per student, but the federal government is now questioning the legality of that state-funded equalization payment.

**2022 funding implications.** The May 2021 Revenue Estimating Conference was optimistic for 2022, 2023, and 2024, projecting the School Aid Fund to close the State's 2021 fiscal year with a fund balance. For 2021-2022 all districts move to the target foundation of $8,700 per pupil; districts already at target receive a $171 per pupil increase from the former target of $8,529, and for hold harmless districts such as Troy the $171 arrives as a $115 per pupil foundation increase plus $56 per pupil of Section 20m funding. Pupil counts revert to the pre-2021 method for 2021-2022, weighted 90 percent fall count and 10 percent spring count. Significant summer 2021 resources supported summer school, credit recovery, and before- and after-school programming through ESSER II plus state aid for innovative summer programming. For 2021-2022 the overall MPSERS contribution rate is expected to increase to 43 percent from 42 percent with the net cost to the district approximating 28 percent.

**Looking forward.** The May 2021 conference projected a 2021 surplus carrying into 2022 with surpluses expected in 2023 and 2024. Factors to monitor include the economic bounce back, the tail-off of federal stimulus over the next two years, the success of returning to in-class instruction, learning loss, enrollment changes, personnel shortages, staffing cost increases, and retirement system cost trends. The next Revenue Estimating Conference will occur in January 2022.

**Grants management and budgeting.** Pandemic programs such as ESSER, GEER, and CRF have increased workload and grants management risk across superintendents and leadership, board members, the business office, staff, information technology, support services, procurement, and facilities. The firm suggests performing a risk assessment of key processes and controls in fiscal 2022. Federal funds carry program end dates laddered through 2024 and are nonrecurring, so recurring uses will require redirecting other revenue or discontinuing programs. Recommended budget practices include multiyear revenue forecasting, monitoring pupil counts, separating recurring contractual payroll costs from variable payroll costs funded by pandemic resources, and budgeting one-time uses of federal and state assistance.

**MPSERS plan net liabilities.** The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2020 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $35 billion, an increase from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, about 3.5 percent, driven primarily by less favorable actuarial experience than assumed. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $5.4 billion at September 30, 2020, down from $7.3 billion at September 30, 2019, a decrease of approximately 26 percent, reflecting a reduction in the health care cost trend rate from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable experience from lower than projected health benefit costs.

**Fund balance.** During 2020-2021 the district's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, equal to about an eight-week operating period; the School District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent and equals approximately 10.3 weeks of operation. Rising CPI and decisions about spending COVID-19 relief funds are cited as pressures on 2021-2022 fund balance.

**Cybersecurity and IT.** Education remains a top ransomware target. The "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act" was introduced in the House in June 2021 and would appropriate $10M yearly for two years to improve district cybersecurity. The letter warns that weak passwords such as "August2021" are easily guessed, raises questions about data location, PII and FERPA data on file-sharing sites or flash drives, and recommends an external vulnerability assessment. It also recommends an IT assessment covering governance, IT staff and organization, external service providers, service delivery, network and device management, cybersecurity policies, and the technology itself, noting many districts use the results as a two- to three-year action plan.

**Accounting and auditing standards ahead.** GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, is effective for the district's June 30, 2022 financial statements and requires lessees to recognize a lease liability and intangible right-of-use asset and lessors to recognize a lease receivable and deferred inflow, with new disclosures; the district must inventory all lease contracts and embedded leases. SAS No. 134, Auditor Reporting and Amendments, issued by the AICPA Auditing Standards Board in May 2019, takes effect for the June 30, 2022 audited financial statements and moves the opinion to the top of the letter, expands the basis of opinion section, explains materiality, defines reasonable assurance, notes that fraud risk exceeds error risk, enhances going concern reporting, describes auditor responsibilities, and introduces key audit matters. The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013 with an exposure draft, "Financial Reporting Model Improvements," issued in June 2020; the comment period ended in February 2021, Plante & Moran submitted comments, and final standards are targeted by June 2022. Proposed changes include additional MD&A information, a budget-to-actual variance column between original and amended budget, terminology shifts from "revenue" and "expenditures" to "inflows" and "outflows of resources," and replacement of modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" using a 12-month horizon rather than the current 60-day receivable rule. Adoption is phased: districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million adopt for the year ending June 30, 2025, and those under $75 million for the year ending June 30, 2026. A related GASB project, the June 2020 preliminary views on "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could produce a standard during 2025.

**Presentation.** "Facilities Condition & Program Assessment Report," Troy School District, presented to the Board of Education under the agenda item "BOE Shared Copy Program & Facilities Assessment Report." The team included the cabinet, administrators, staff, students, and parents.

**Two areas of focus.** The Facilities Condition Assessment covered interior and exterior infrastructure and sites against code and standards, sorted into categories of 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+, and 15+ years. The Program Assessment identified barriers and deficiencies in buildings and sites that impede delivering education in the most optimum way today and in the future.

**Process.** Kick-off meeting March 2021; facilities toured March through August 2021; status meetings; project worklists developed; items quantified and cost estimates developed; needs categorized and prioritized.

**Fun facts.** Roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; average building age 48 years; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**System findings and cost ranges.** Roofing, with a typical 20-year lifespan and aging roofs, $10-15 Million. Architectural systems, covering aging doors, flooring, and furnishings such as cabinets, gym equipment, and marker boards, $40-45 Million. Mechanical systems, with a 20-year equipment lifespan, aging boilers, aging classroom unit ventilators, and malfunctioning plumbing fixtures, $45-50 Million. Electrical systems, including LED lighting upgrades with energy rebates and operational savings and replacement of emergency/exit lighting, $30-35 Million, illustrated with existing and new lighting in the Troy High School Media Center. Site work paving, with a 20-year asphalt lifespan, replacing aging parking lots and sidewalks, $20-23 Million. Playgrounds and athletics, assessed on condition, age appropriateness, and safety, $5-7 Million.

| Roofing Systems | $10-15 Million |
| Architectural Systems | $40-45 Million |
| Mechanical Systems | $45-50 Million |
| Electrical Systems | $30-35 Million |
| Site Work | $25-30 Million |

| Near Future Needs (4-6 years) | $90-100 Million |
| Future Needs (7-10 years) | $85-95 Million |
| **Total** | **$220-250 Million** |

**Program assessment.** Program decisions can absorb facilities needs, and the program assessment carries no dollar amount, which comes later in design work. Steps were vision setting and discovery, defining the ideal program, and evaluating existing schools against that ideal. Leaders cited making thinking visible, the 6 C's of learning (collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, character/compassion, citizenship), project-based learning, competency-based learning, social emotional learning, multi-tiered systems of supports, and experiential learning through internships, career pathways, and CTE. Teachers named team collaborative work, one-on-one time, mobile technology, and workshop instruction, and valued good lighting, natural light, and decluttered, flexible space. Among secondary students, 85.7% agree that more connections to real-life experiences should be provided. A workshop with Dr. Tony Wagner explored deep learning, its barriers (money, resources, time; staff and parent readiness; physical structure and furniture; state mandated credits and time requirements), and its ideal space.

**Attributes and guiding principles.** Every school is documented in spreadsheet format with detailed notes for review by the Facilities Review Committee, graded Good, Needs Improvement, or Poor on attributes including smaller learning communities, classroom size, ability to adapt, collaboration spaces, connection to the outdoors, entry image, traffic separation on site, appropriate playgrounds, teacher collaboration spaces, spaces for physical activities, athletic/recreation/community facilities, spaces for fine and performing arts, spaces for community partnerships, universal design, acoustics, environmental control, natural light, integration of technology, and mobile and varied furniture. Guiding principles address curiosity and movement, safe and welcoming access, gross motor development, smaller learning communities, flexible spaces, abundant natural light, eco-friendly schools, professional space for staff, district brand image, universal design accessibility, shared collaboration spaces, career exploration and community partnerships, and well-being and sensory needs.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Ninety-two-slide presentation titled "Facilities Condition & Program Assessment Report" for Troy School District, brought to the Board of Education meeting of October 5, 2021 under the agenda title "BOE Shared Copy Program & Facilities Assessment Report." The team slide lists cabinet, administrators, staff, students, and parents.

**Two areas of focus.** The Facilities Condition Assessment examined interior and exterior infrastructure and sites, code and standards, using categories of 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+, and 15+. The Program Assessment focused on identifying barriers and deficiencies in the district's school buildings and sites that prevent or impede delivering education in the most optimum way today and in the future.

**Process and agenda.** The condition assessment agenda covered overview, fun facts, facility findings (roofing, architectural, mechanical, electrical, civil, playground/athletics), cost summary, and next steps. The kick-off meeting was held in March 2021, facilities were toured from March through August 2021, status meetings were held, project worklists were developed, items were quantified and cost estimates developed, and needs were categorized and prioritized.

**Fun facts about the district's physical plant.** Roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, described as over 50 acres. Approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures. Over 4,300 doors. Over 2 million square feet of parking lot. 1.7 million square feet of roofing. Average building age of 48 years old. Approximately 500 acres of property, described as roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**Roofing.** Typical roof lifespan is 20 years and the district's roofs are aging. Cost range $10-15 Million.

**Architectural systems.** Aging doors, aging flooring, and aging furnishings including cabinets, gym equipment, and marker boards. Cost range $40-45 Million.

**Mechanical systems.** Mechanical equipment lifespan is 20 years; findings include aging boilers, aging classroom unit ventilators, and malfunctioning plumbing fixtures. Cost range $45-50 Million.

**Electrical systems.** Opportunities include energy rebates and operational savings, upgrading lighting to energy efficient LED, and replacing emergency and exit lighting. Cost range $30-35 Million. Before-and-after images show Troy High School Media Center existing lighting and Troy High Media Center new lighting.

**Site work, paving.** Typical lifespan of asphalt is 20 years; recommendations are to replace aging parking lots and replace sidewalks. Cost range $20-23 Million.

**Site work, playgrounds and athletics.** Assessment completed based on condition, age appropriateness, and safety. Cost range $5-7 Million.

**Cost summary by category.** Roofing Systems $10-15 Million; Architectural Systems $40-45 Million; Mechanical Systems $45-50 Million; Electrical Systems $30-35 Million; Site Work $25-30 Million; Furniture, Kitchen Equipment $23-28 Million; Buses $12 Million; Technology Devices $35 Million; total $220-250 Million.

**Cost summary by priority.** Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55 Million; Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100 Million; Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95 Million; total $220-250 Million.

**Program assessment framing.** The presentation stresses the interplay between facilities needs and program needs, noting that some program decisions may impact and "take care of" facilities needs; the example given is that design of a new instructional space will address the need to update lighting and architectural systems. The program assessment is not accompanied by a dollar amount, which comes in design work moving forward. The sequence is vision setting and discovery, understanding TSD vision and goals and looking to the future of education, defining the ideal program, and evaluating existing schools against the ideal future program of spaces.

**Feedback shared by leaders.** Themes include making thinking visible; the 6 C's of learning - collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, character/compassion, and citizenship; motivating learners to explore information in order to construct new ideas, identify new relationships, and create new models of thinking and behavior; dream and imagination; project based learning leveraging real-world partnerships, scenarios and applications; descriptive grading and alternative assessment; character education; responsive/workshop instruction; social emotional learning; multi-tiered system of supports and the "whole child"; growth mindset; experiential learning through internships, career pathways and CTE; competency based learning with mastery learning and self-paced flexibility; and authentic learning or learning by doing.

**What teachers reported.** Top instructional practices were team collaborative work, one on one with teacher, learning with mobile technology, social emotional learning, independent study, performance based learning, project-based learning, workshop, peer-to-peer, and classroom libraries. Students are most engaged when emotional well-being is prioritized, content extends to students' lives, there is collaboration with peers, opportunities for choice, readily accessible resources, curiosity is piqued, students can see effort paying off, and individualized expectations are visible. Attributes that make a teacher want to be in a space are good lighting, natural light, clean and decluttered, inspiring, active and allowing movement, connection to others, and flexibility to change the space.

**Elementary student responses.** To be successful students said it is important to work well as a team, be creative, and think about hard questions and solve big problems. They learn best working quietly on their own, talking to other students about what they are learning, building projects together, and when they feel happy, and ranked learning with friends, with their teacher, and with their family in that order of importance.

**Secondary student responses.** Interest in going to school is affected by subject matter connecting to interests, fun activities, choosing where and how to work best, opportunities to develop talents, comfortable environments, confidence from succeeding, awareness of expectations, feeling safe to explore ideas without fear of failure, opportunities to work alone, and a flexible class schedule. 85.7% agree that more connections to real-life experiences should be provided to students. Spaces that positively impact learning are social commons, flexible learning studios, partnership space where real life skills can be shared, private space, outdoor spaces, and lab/maker spaces; students are most comfortable with soft comfortable furniture, clean and de-cluttered rooms, access to food and drink throughout the day, and quiet and calm space.

**Dr. Tony Wagner workshop.** Administrators answered five questions. On the most important characteristics of deep learning: inquiry and project based learning; collaboration and feedback; critical thinking with access to resources, tools and technology; foundational feelings of safety and connection to topic; student voice, agency and exhibition; and learning from failure. On activities that lead to deep learning: working collaboratively on a team, encouraging creativity and thinking outside the box, demonstrating, challenging and defending ideas, and spaces and access to research. On current barriers or roadblocks: money, resources and time; preparing staff and parents for change, culture shift and buy in; the physical structure of the building and furniture; state mandated credits and time requirements; and the current system's mindset, tradition and risk tolerance. On the ideal space: flexible and moveable, more natural light, calming colors and tones with students first and safety, a "watering hole" place to collaborate, places for students to showcase work, and space allowing collaboration of students and staff from multiple disciplines. On what success looks like: evidence of student engagement, inspiring future learning, students feeling passionate and finding meaning and purpose, other schools coming to learn from Troy, relationships developing between students and staff, and everyone feeling comfortable sharing ideas.

**Attributes of modern learning environments.** Every school is documented in spreadsheet format with detailed notes for review by the Facilities Review Committee, with a program assessment grade across all buildings and all attributes rated Good, Needs Improvement, or Poor. Attributes assessed include smaller learning communities (systematic organization of spaces sized for a small subset of the school population, adjacency supporting seamless movement and non-traditional schedules, and a menu of spaces encouraging subject-matter cross fertilization); classroom size (space for flexible furniture and student movement, project-based, peer-to-peer and student-centered learning); ability to adapt (spaces easily adapted for current and future programs, with technology and infrastructure supporting fast delivery shifts); collaboration spaces (adjacent to instructional spaces, configured for passive supervision, organized with variety of group size, horizontal surface size and content sharing); connection to the outdoors; entry image (clearly visible and branded secure entry, visible inside and outside, directing visitors to staff/help, consistent brand); traffic separation on site (separate bus and parent drop off, safe traffic flow, dedicated visitor parking, dedicated entrances for academics, athletics and performing arts); appropriate playgrounds (safe and sustainable materials, accessibility, supporting active bodies); teacher collaboration spaces assigned to specific Professional Learning Communities; spaces for physical activities accessible in all weather and supporting social emotional and wellness goals including formal gym class and wellness uses such as meditation and yoga; athletic, recreation and community facilities (safe and in good condition, practice and match/game space, adequate size for players and spectators, equity across genders, easily secured for community use, addressing recreation as well as athletics); spaces for fine and performing arts with practice, gallery and performance space; spaces for community partnerships affording real-life training, accessible to industry professionals and after-hours use, with partnership branding opportunities; universal design; acoustics (surface materials lowering sound reverberation time, reduced background noise, improved speech intelligibility, mechanical systems designed to reduce background noise, and intentional quiet/isolation spaces); environmental control (on demand temperature, ventilation and air quality adjustability, varied lighting solutions with adjustable levels and color temperatures, displayed energy use information); natural light (daylit spaces supporting circadian rhythms, energy reduction through daylighting, views supporting creative thinking); integration of technology (students sharing content from devices, content clearly visible to all learners); and mobile, varied furniture that is easily reconfigured, inclusive of all body sizes and abilities, and encourages movement.

**Guiding principles.** Provide spaces that encourage curiosity, movement and exploration; convenient, direct, safe and welcoming access for students and parents; interior and exterior spaces for gross motor development; organize schools into smaller learning communities supporting belonging, collaboration, inclusion and equity; provide flexible, adaptable and stimulating learning spaces; provide abundant natural light in all instructional spaces; make schools eco-friendly with interaction with the natural environment; provide professional space for teachers and staff to encourage teaming, collaboration, interaction and observation; create a strong, progressive, inviting and innovative visual image promoting the district brand; ensure accessibility for all students and staff through universal design; provide shared collaboration spaces for individual, small group and large groups; create spaces for career exploration and community partnerships supporting real-world experiential learning; design spaces supporting well-being including quiet and sensory spaces; create spaces for interdisciplinary collaboration; provide flexible furnishings to transform existing classrooms into flexible learning studios; improve shared spaces for fine and performing arts, athletics and other performances and competitions for students and the community; assure seamless integration of technology; and transform existing playgrounds into outdoor spaces reinforcing curricular goals and a positive relationship with nature.

**Next steps.** A slide asks "Questions for TMP?" The Facilities Review Committee will have 57 members drawn from community members from all areas of the district plus teachers, administrators, and students. Its first meeting is October 12th, with an update to be given at the BOE Workshop on December 7th.

**Instrument and parties**
First Amendment to the Amended and Restated Pupil Transportation and Transportation Fleet Maintenance Services Contract, entered into as of July 1, 2025 (the Effective Date), attached to and made part of the Contract dated July 1, 2022. Parties: TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, a Michigan general powers school district, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098; and FIRST STUDENT, INC., a Delaware corporation, 191 Rosa Parks Street, Suite 800, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202. Agenda item 3.b, June 3, 2025 meeting. Document control stamp 282059785.v1.

**Renewal Term**
Under Section 2.2, the School District exercises its option to extend, with the Parties agreeing to modify Section 2.2 and extend for two (2) years, commencing July 1, 2025 and expiring June 30, 2027. Thereafter the District may extend by up to one (1) additional year on a year-to-year basis, subject to written approval in its sole and absolute discretion (the Extension Term). Extension Term rates are to be mutually agreed under Section 10.3. The Contractor is stated to have no expectation of a contract beyond the Renewal Term.

**Other amended terms**
Exhibit B is replaced in its entirety. Sections 19.1 and 19.2 (Notices) are amended: notices to the District go to the Superintendent, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098, copy to Jeremy S. Motz, Esq., Clark Hill PLC, 220 Park Street, Suite 200, Birmingham, Michigan 48009; notices to the Contractor go to First Student, Inc., Attn: Area General Manager, 120 Hart Avenue, Troy, Michigan 48098, copy to FirstGroup American, Attn: General Counsel, 191 Rosa Parks Street, 8th Floor, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202. A Change In Law clause terminates the District's obligations if federal or state law makes payment of the Rates illegal, impracticable or impossible. Further modification requires a writing signed by both Parties; the Contract is ratified and reaffirmed except as modified, with the First Amendment controlling in a conflict; execution may be in counterparts.

**Exhibit B charges and rates (Transportation & Bus Maintenance Services)**

| Pricing parameter | # of Routes | 2025-2026 | 2026-2027 |
|---|---|---|---|
| General Education Route Daily Route Charge | 33 | $306.78 | $334.39 |
| Special Needs Route Daily Route Charge - In District | 17 | $454.93 | $495.87 |
| Special Needs Route Daily Route Charge - Out of District | 7 | $454.93 | $495.87 |
| Mid-Day Runs & Shuttles (hourly, if not attached to Route) | 24 | $78.33 | $85.38 |
| Special Needs Route Daily Route Charge - Summer | 20 | $379.63 | $413.80 |
| Extra-Curricular/Athletic Trips (per hour) | Varies | $69.91 | $76.20 |

Footnotes state the charges include all costs and expenses for maintenance services for the buses; the Special Needs Daily Route Charge includes Out-District and Wing Lake Routes; the General Education Daily Route Charge also includes Summer General Education Routes; and extra-curricular/athletic trips carry a 1-hour minimum charge. White Fleet maintenance labor rates (parts at cost) are left to be mutually agreed before services are performed.

**Pricing assumptions**
Daily Route Charges assume an average Daily Route Time of 6.0 hours per day per Route, measured gate to gate from the District's Transportation Facility. Field, athletic and extra-curricular trips are invoiced hourly in quarter-hour increments. Pricing assumes 175 days per academic year of regular route service, with a 175-day Academic School Year Minimum; one free dry run per Route is provided before school year start-up. Snow days are billed at 80% of the Daily Route Charge when driver pay is documented, otherwise 40%; intermittent closures at 40%; extended closures beyond ten consecutive school days at 70% or 25% depending on driver employment status. The District supplies fuel. A route-volume change of 10% or greater is deemed material and triggers good-faith renegotiation.

The First Amendment to the Amended and Restated Pupil Transportation and Transportation Fleet Maintenance Services Contract is entered into as of July 1, 2025, designated the Effective Date, and is attached to and made a part of the Amended and Restated Pupil Transportation and Transportation Fleet Maintenance Services Contract dated July 1, 2022. The Parties are TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, described as a Michigan general powers school district with an address of 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098, and FIRST STUDENT, INC., a Delaware corporation with an address of 191 Rosa Parks Street, Suite 800, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202. Section 1, Renewal Term of Contract, recites that pursuant to Section 2.2 of the Contract the School District desires to exercise its option to extend, provided that the Parties agree to modify Section 2.2 and extend the Contract for two (2) years, commencing July 1, 2025 and expiring on June 30, 2027, defined as the Renewal Term. Thereafter the School District has the option to extend by up to one (1) additional year on a year-to-year basis, subject to the written approval of the School District in its sole and absolute discretion, defined as the Extension Term. Rates for any Extension Term are to be mutually agreed in accordance with Section 10.3 of the Contract. Nothing requires the School District to exercise the option, and the Contractor is stated to have no expectation of a contract beyond the Renewal Term or any exercised Extension Term.

Section 2, Rates, provides that as of the Effective Date the Rates set forth in Exhibit B are updated and Exhibit B of the Contract is replaced in its entirety with the Exhibit B attached to the First Amendment. Section 3, Notices, amends Sections 19.1 and 19.2 in their entirety while leaving the remainder of Section 19 unchanged. Under amended Section 19.1, required notices to the School District go to the Superintendent, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098, with a copy to Jeremy S. Motz, Esq., Clark Hill PLC, 220 Park Street, Suite 200, Birmingham, Michigan 48009. Under amended Section 19.2, required notices to the Contractor go to First Student, Inc., Attn: Area General Manager, 120 Hart Avenue, Troy, Michigan 48098, with a copy to FirstGroup American, Attn: General Counsel, 191 Rosa Parks Street, 8th Floor, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202.

Section 4, Change In Law, provides that if any federal or state law, rule, regulation or ordinance is enacted, modified or otherwise changed that would make the School District's payment of the Rates and fees illegal, impracticable or impossible to pay, the School District's obligations under the First Amendment and the Contract cease and are not in effect. Section 5 limits further modification to a written agreement signed by both Parties. Section 6 states in capitals that the Contract is ratified and reaffirmed and continues in full force and effect except as modified, and that in the event of a conflict the First Amendment controls. Section 7 permits execution in one or more counterparts, each an original and all together constituting one document.

Exhibit B, captioned Contractor's Pricing, opens with pricing assumptions and conditions. Daily Route Charges are billed per Route per day; a Route includes the AM tier runs, Mid-Day or Shuttle runs if any, and PM tier runs operated by the same bus as part of the same Route package, and a Mid-Day or Shuttle run built into an AM/PM package is included in the daily Route charge while one not incorporated into a package is charged at the applicable listed rate. Daily Route Charges are based on an average daily Route time of 6.0 hours of service per day per Route, the Daily Route Time, calculated gate to gate from the School District's Transportation Facility. All Field Trips, Athletic Trips and Extra-Curricular Trips are calculated and invoiced on an hourly basis or portion thereof in quarter-hour increments.

The Contractor's pricing and fixed costs assume the School District operates school and requires regular route home-to-school transportation for 175 days per academic year for general education routing. The Contractor will conduct one (1) dry run for each Route in advance of school year start-up without charge. A 175-day Academic School Year Minimum applies to regularly scheduled Routes, with the academic year running from the first day of school in September until the last day of school in June and excluding summer transportation. The School District is not charged for Routes on days school is not in session or when Other Transportation Services are not operated, provided cancellation follows Section 10.1, subject to stated exceptions. For snow days, the School District is charged 80% of the Daily Route Charge for each Route not operated provided the Contractor demonstrates that all bus drivers are paid at their normal rate for their normally scheduled route; if the Contractor fails to pay or document such payment, the charge drops to the 40% rate. For intermittent closures, where the School District operates less than 180 per academic school year requiring Transportation Services because of power outages or similar intermittent events, the charge is 40% of the Daily Route Charge for each Route not operated less than 175 days.

Extended closures are defined as a period extending beyond ten (10) consecutive school days. Where the District replaces in-person instruction with hybrid or remote learning, it agrees to pay 70% of the then-current cost per Route per day for each Route not operated, provided that a qualified and trained bus driver is assigned and in active employment status receiving at least the driver's daily minimum pay rate; that all other Contractor staff positions, namely the Site Manager, Dispatcher and Router (the Management Personnel) and one (1) Mechanic (the Maintenance Personnel), remain in active employment status at full pay; that all wages are paid at prevailing or regular rates rather than a discounted hourly wage; and that the Contractor performs all other Transportation and Maintenance Services within contract parameters. If the Driver is not in active employment status receiving full pay, the rate is 25% of the then-current cost per Route per day. The School District may elect to operate under the 25% provision at its option during an extended closure. As a condition of payment, no later than five (5) days after each weekly or bi-weekly payroll cycle the Contractor must make available for inspection all books, records and data related to wages paid to personnel assigned to the School District; if verification shows terms were not met or that personnel are no longer employed, laid off or furloughed, charges are adjusted and the Contractor must reimburse overpayments. If the District operates under the 70% provision and also runs a food delivery program, athletic or extra-curricular routes or other auxiliary transportation, the Contractor uses staff from its to/from school or extra trips service team without additional fee unless services exceed contemplated parameters.

The Contractor's rates assume the School District provides the necessary fuel, and the Contractor is liable for all costs and expenses associated with misuse of that fuel. If changes to District operations cause a material increase or decrease in the volume of Routes, the Parties will convene and negotiate in good faith changes to Route Rates and Charges, with material defined as a change of equal to or greater than 10%. Adjustments to charges for any Extension Term follow Section 10.3.

**Form and association**
Michigan High School Athletic Association membership resolution for 2025-26, presented as item 6E on the June 17, 2025 Troy Board of Education agenda. The MHSAA is located at 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, telephone (517) 332-5046. It is described as a voluntary, nonprofit corporation of public, private and parochial junior high/middle and senior high schools whose boards of education or governing bodies have applied for and received membership on behalf of their secondary schools. Completed forms are to be saved and sent to camala@mhsaa.com as an attachment, with one signed copy returned and one retained.

**Terms of membership**
The association sponsors statewide tournaments and makes eligibility rules for participation. Boards that wish to host or participate must join and agree to abide by and enforce MHSAA rules, regulations and qualifications on eligibility, game rules and tournament policies, procedures and schedules. Participation in MHSAA postseason tournaments is conditioned on high schools adhering to at least the minimum standards of Regulation I and the maximum limitations of Regulation II in all MHSAA tournament sports. **Resolution language**
The resolution covers the year August 1, 2025 through July 31, 2026 and enrolls the named schools as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc. and to participate in its approved interschool athletic activities. The board delegates supervision and control of those activities to the Superintendent or designee, accepts the association's Constitution and By-Laws, and adopts the rules, regulations and interpretations in the current Handbook as minimum standards and as the governing code, agreeing to primary enforcement. Schools may join at the 6th-grade level to reach the 15-student minimum whether or not 6th-graders participate. Districts are not required to hold junior high/middle school membership or to sponsor 6th-grade athletics. If a listed junior high/middle school sponsors a 6th-grade team in any sport or lets a 6th-grader play with 7th and 8th graders, all of Regulations III and IV apply to all 6th-graders in all sports involving 6th-graders on that school's teams; if no 6th-graders participate in a sport, MHSAA rules do not apply in that sport.

Approximately 14 members of the audience attended. The K-12 Alliance of Michigan, through Oakland Schools, asked member districts to pass board resolutions supporting the IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021 (HR 5984) ahead of a March 10 trip to Washington, D.C., noting that Congress committed in 1975 to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost of special education but that the federal investment is today less than 14 percent. Superintendent Richard Machesky forwarded the alert to Board President Karl Schmidt on February 7, 2022, recommending the item be discussed Thursday and placed on the February agenda; Schmidt replied "okiedokie."

Chain of Correspondence
A three-message email thread. The top message is from Karl Schmidt (Troy Board of Education President) to Richard Machesky, copying Judy Holmes, sent Monday, February 7, 2022 at 4:36:01 PM, reading simply "okiedokie." It responds to a forward from Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. (rmachesky2@troy.k12.mi.us, office phone 248-823-4003), sent Monday, February 7, 2022 at 12:28 PM, which stated: "I would also recommend we discuss this on Thursday and prepare to have it on our February agenda." The underlying alert came from the OCSA listserv (ocsa-request@lists.oakland.k12.mi.us) on behalf of Nicole Christian, sent Thursday, February 3, 2022 at 4:57 PM to the OCSA ListServ, copying OSCabinet, David Randels, and Lisa Hansknecht, and forwarded on behalf of David Randels of Oakland Schools.

The Ask
K-12 Alliance members will meet with members of Congress in Washington, D.C. in March to push for full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), and the alert seeks evidence of broad Michigan support. Districts are asked to work with their school boards to pass resolutions in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act; a sample school board resolution (Sample School Board Resolution.docx) was provided, with the request that boards pass it or a similar resolution at their next meeting if at all possible.

Funding Background
When Congress enacted IDEA in 1975 to ensure all students with disabilities have access to quality public education, it committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost schools would face to provide those services. Today the federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent. The IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021 (HR 5984) would require yearly increases to funding for IDEA programs so that the federal government reaches an annual appropriation of 40% of the cost of special education services within the next 10 years.

Logistics
Passed resolutions are to be shared with Katie Whitman-Herzer by email at katie@k12michigan.org. The Alliance will compile the passed board resolutions and bring them to Washington on March 10th to share with members of Congress. Signatories are Robert McCann, Executive Director, and Katie Whitman-Herzer, Administrative Director, The K-12 Alliance of Michigan, P.O. Box 16085, Lansing, Michigan 48901, United States.

Attached Media Clips
The newsletter closes with links to Michigan education coverage: Betsy DeVos backing Michigan petitions for a voucher-like school choice program; Whitmer's proposal to cut taxes and boost schools with Michigan GOP agreement; a Michigan bill to let college students lead classes to curb the teacher shortage; a new Oxford High shooting lawsuit seeking to limit government immunity protection for public schools; Whitmer's call for schools to return to in-person learning; Whitmer and lawmakers exploring ways to ensure in-person classes amid the pandemic; polling on using COVID-19 windfall funds for tutoring and mental health first; Democrats pushing to allow local boards to meet virtually again; districts running out of snow days; and nonprofit and national money pouring into voter ID, public health, and school initiatives. A standard Oakland Schools caution notes the email originated outside the organization.

Substance of the appeal. Addressed to "K-12 Alliance Members," the alert states that in March, members from the K-12 Alliance will be meeting with members of Congress in Washington, DC to push for full funding for the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), and that the Alliance needs help demonstrating the broad support behind this effort in Michigan. It recounts that when Congress enacted IDEA in 1975 to ensure all students with disabilities have access to quality public education, Congress committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost schools would face to provide those services. Today, the alert states, the federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent, and "it's long-past time for that to change."

The legislation. The IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021, identified as HR 5984, would require yearly increases to funding for IDEA programs so that the federal government reaches an annual appropriation of 40% of the cost of special education services within the next 10 years, described as finally fulfilling the obligation made back in 1975.

Requested action. While the Alliance works with Michigan's Congressional delegation, it asks recipients to work with their school boards to pass resolutions in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act. The Alliance created a sample resolution, referenced as the attachment "Sample School Board Resolution.docx," and asks that boards pass it or a similar resolution at their next meeting if at all possible. The stated goal is to go to Washington in March with resolutions from as many districts as possible, both to show the level of support for the action and to convey the meaningful change it would make in schools going forward.

Submission logistics. Passed resolutions can be shared with Katie Whitman-Herzer by emailing her at katie@k12michigan.org. The Alliance will compile and bring all of the passed board resolutions to Washington on March 10th and share them with members of Congress. The message is signed by Robert McCann, Executive Director, and Katie Whitman-Herzer, Administrative Director.

Sender identification and footers. The sending organization is The K-12 Alliance of Michigan, P.O. Box 16085, Lansing, Michigan 48901, United States, with an Unsubscribe link and the note that the recipient received the email as a member of The K-12 Alliance of Michigan. An Oakland Schools security banner reads: "CAUTION: This email originated from outside of Oakland Schools. Do NOT click on any links or open attachments unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe."

Media clips appended to the newsletter. The alert carries a "Media Clips" section linking to contemporaneous Michigan education coverage: "Betsy DeVos backs Michigan petitions for voucher-like school choice program" (bridgemi.com); "Whitmer: Cut taxes, boost schools. Michigan GOP agrees, but devil's in details" (bridgemi.com, michigan-government section); "Michigan bill would let college students lead classes to curb teacher shortage" (bridgemi.com, talent-education section); "New Oxford High shooting lawsuit hopes to limit government immunity protection for public schools" (mlive.com, public-interest, 2022/01); "Whitmer says schools should return to in-person learning. Education advocates want state support to do it." (mlive.com, public-interest, 2022/01); "Whitmer, lawmakers exploring more ways to ensure in-person classes amid pandemic" (freep.com, politics, January 26, 2022); "Poll: Michigan schools should use COVID-19 windfall for tutoring, mental health first" (freep.com, education, January 28, 2022, referencing ESSER funds); "Democrats push to allow local boards to meet virtually again as COVID surges in Michigan" (mlive.com, public-interest, 2022/01); "Michigan districts are running out of snow days. What happens now?" (bridgemi.com, talent-education); and "Nonprofit, national money pour into voter ID, public health, school initiatives" (detroitnews.com, politics, February 2, 2022).

Significance for the Board. The packet item documents the chain of custody by which an Oakland Schools / K-12 Alliance advocacy request reached the Troy Board of Education, and records that the Superintendent and the Board President agreed to place a supporting resolution on the February 2022 Board agenda, consistent with the Alliance's March 10 deadline for collecting district resolutions.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education, Board Meeting minutes, November 17, 2020, held remotely via Zoom Webinar with public notice posted for remote community participation. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; adjournment at 8:45 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (GH/jh).

**Attendance**
Present via Zoom videoconference in addition to Mr. Schmidt: Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson, all connecting from locations in Troy, Michigan. Also present: Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Roncone, Haezebrouck, House, Pagel and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 48 additional members of the audience.

**Recognition — TSD Mission Moment**
The Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) Diversity, Inclusion, Justice, and Equity (DIJE) subcommittee awarded a DIJE professional development grant to Troy High School English teachers Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick and Valerie Valentino. Their reading program includes "Black Appetite. White Food" by Jamila Lyiscott, "We Got This." by Cornelius Miner, "The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook" by Lorena German, "Educating Activist Allies" by Katy Swalwell, and "Linguistic Justice" by April Baker-Bell.

**Public Communication**
Andrew Rodman, Troy resident and parent of two Martell Elementary School students, addressed the Board about moving elementary students back to remote learning and when they plan to return to in-seat instruction.

**Actions**

| No. | Item | Mover / Support | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20-084 | Consent agenda items A, B, C: minutes of the October 6, 2020 Workshop; minutes of the October 20, 2020 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report - September 2020 | Hauff / Hammond | Yes 7, No 0 |
