| 20-086 | School bus bid awarded to Hoekstra Transportation, $1,687,276.00, as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund | Philippart / Anne | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 20-087 | Reconfirmation of the District's COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan | Wilson / Philippart | Yes 6, No 1 (Hammond) |
| 20-088 | Resolution on Senate Bill 1108 / Open Meetings Act | Philippart / Hauff | Yes 7, No 0 |

**Discussion**
On the bus purchase, the Board discussed end of life cycle for buses and resale value, and grants for electric buses; Mr. West explained electric buses would be cost-prohibitive at this time. Dr. Machesky gave an extended learning plan update with PowerPoint slides on rising COVID case counts in Michigan and Oakland County, with additional updates from Ms. Birmingham, Mrs. Griffor and Mrs. DiPilato.

**Open Meetings Act resolution (20-088)**
Citing Governor Whitmer's framework and the Americans with Disabilities Act reasonable accommodation clause, the resolution urges the Legislature to amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) so local public bodies set their own remote-participation policies, or at minimum to extend remote attendance for medical conditions and states of emergency or disaster in addition to military service, and directs the Board Secretary to transmit copies within five business days to Senator Mallory McMorrow, Representative Padma Kuppa, Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, and the Michigan Association of School Boards.

**Comments and reports**
Board comments from Hammond, Wilson, Philippart (TFEE raffle for $1,000 worth of gift cards, tickets $5 each), Gottlieb, Hauff and Anne. Dr. Machesky congratulated Bemis Elementary School on a second National Blue Ribbon School recognition. Mr. Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for December 1 at 6:00 p.m. via Zoom.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Official minutes of a Board Meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, dated November 17, 2020, held remotely via Zoom Webinar. A public notice was posted to allow community members to participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present via Zoom videoconference were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson, all connecting remotely from locations in Troy, Michigan. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Roncone, Haezebrouck, House, Pagel and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 48 additional members of the audience. The minutes were submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION. The TSD Mission Moment honored the Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) Diversity, Inclusion, Justice & Equity (DIJE) Grant Award to Troy High School English teachers. The MCTE DIJE subcommittee awarded Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick and Valerie Valentino of Troy High School a DIJE professional development grant. The grant's goal is to support Michigan English teachers across the state as they engage in professional development they design that privileges diversity, inclusion, justice, and equity work. The five teachers created a program of reading and learning supporting their commitment to "disrupting stock stories, stereotypes, and westernized narratives." Their selected texts are "Black Appetite. White Food: Issues of Race, Voice and Justice Within and Beyond the Classroom" by Jamila Lyiscott; "We Got This.: Equity, Access, and the Quest to Be Who Our Students Need Us to Be" by Cornelius Miner; "The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook" by Lorena German; "Educating Activist Allies: Social Justice Pedagogy with the Suburban and Urban Elite" by Katy Swalwell; and "Linguistic Justice: Black Language, Literacy, Identity, and Pedagogy" by April Baker-Bell. Their intention is to use the concepts and practice from the readings to plan learning for students to build community and engage in rich activist lives.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION. Andrew Rodman, Troy resident and parent of two students who attend Martell Elementary School, addressed the Board about the decision to move elementary students back to remote learning and when they plan to return to in-seat instruction.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA (Resolution 20-084). It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B and C on the consent agenda: minutes of the October 6, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 20, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for September 2020. On roll call vote, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff and Philippart all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

PERSONNEL and CURRICULUM sections contained no items.

BUSINESS - Building Signage (Resolution 20-085). It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for signage for the refurbishment of the school messaging sign at Athens High School and new messaging signs at the Troy Preschool and Troy Learning Center be awarded to Johnson Sign Company in the amount of $92,000 (inclusive of 6% contingency), and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and/or the Sinking Fund. On roll call vote, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BUSINESS - Bus Purchase (Resolution 20-086). It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $1,687,276.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. There was discussion about the end of life cycle for buses and how much money the District could sell them for, and about looking into grants for electric buses; however, Mr. West explained that electric buses would be cost-prohibitive at this time. On roll call vote, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Public Communication on non-agenda items: None.

OTHER - Extended Learning Plan. Dr. Machesky shared an update on the District's extended learning plan and provided PowerPoint slides showing the most recent numbers in COVID cases and how much they had been climbing in Michigan and in Oakland County. Ms. Birmingham, Mrs. Griffor and Mrs. DiPilato also shared updates from their respective areas, followed by further discussion among Board members.

Reconfirmation of COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan (Resolution 20-087). The minutes recite that Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support all schools in Michigan as they plan for a return of Pre-K through Post High School education in the fall, and that under this order Michigan school districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan laying out how they will cope with the disease across the various phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan. Each district must submit a reconfirmation plan to its Board of Education for approval on a monthly basis, and once approved must post its Preparedness Plan on the district website home page for public access. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Troy Board of Education approve the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan. On roll call vote, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond No, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes. Yes: 6, No: 1.

Open Meetings Act Resolution (Resolution 20-088). It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff. The whereas clauses state that Michigan Senate Bill 1108 of 2020 amended the State's Open Meetings Act to restrict the reasons a member of a public body may attend a public meeting remotely beginning January 1, 2021; that advancing technology enabled school districts across the State to meet remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic, develop and implement plans to educate students safely and effectively, and ensure safe and effective public participation; that the restrictions in Senate Bill 1108 allow remote attendance after December 31, 2021 only for absence due to military duty; that threats to public health and other disasters will not vanish on December 31, 2020, and that contagious diseases, flooding, tornadoes, acts of terrorism or other causes occurring after that date could make it unsafe or impossible for public bodies to meet in person or for some members to attend in person; that not allowing an immune-compromised member of a public body to participate remotely would be a clear violation of the Reasonable Accommodation clause of the Federal Americans with Disabilities Act; and that decisions about situations meriting remote attendance are best determined by the local body and the community it represents rather than the State Legislature. The resolved clauses urge the Legislature ideally to amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to include a provision requiring local public bodies to set their own policies regarding remote meeting participation based on the needs and priorities of their own local communities rather than dictating universal policy without regard to local control; urge the Legislature at a minimum to amend Sec. 3a(b) to extend indefinitely its provisions allowing remote attendance to accommodate absence due to a medical condition or a statewide or local state of emergency or state of disaster, in addition to military service, and to add accommodations for family emergencies and work obligations; and direct the Board Secretary to transmit copies of the resolution within five business days of adoption to Senator Mallory McMorrow, Representative Padma Kuppa, Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, and the Michigan Association of School Boards. On roll call vote, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne and Gottlieb all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BOARD COMMENTS. Mrs. Hammond spoke about events during the last Board meeting, said it was unfairly presented, and stated she will continue to advocate for what she believes in. Dr. Wilson thanked teachers and administrators for their hard work. Dr. Philippart announced that the TFEE is holding a pandemic-safe fundraiser offering a raffle for $1,000 worth of gift cards, with tickets available at $5 each. Mr. Gottlieb thanked TSD staff and fellow board members. Mr. Hauff thanked veterans for their sacrifice and service, thanked the Central Office staff and teachers, and said oneTROY is the greatest school district in Michigan. Mrs. Anne thanked everyone for their work during difficult times.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Pranay Gupta, student representative from International Academy - East, reported on students learning virtually at his school. Nathania Nartey, student representative from Athens High School, reported on happenings now that students are 100% virtual. Sejal Patel, student representative from Troy High School, and Carleton Thomas, student representative from Troy College & Career High School, were not in attendance.

Dr. Machesky thanked the Board for its continued efforts and support of the LIVE program, congratulated Bemis Elementary School on being recognized as a National Blue Ribbon School for the second time, and wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving. Mr. Schmidt wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving and announced the next Board Workshop for December 1 at 6:00 p.m. via Zoom.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting was adjourned at 8:45 p.m.

A public notice was posted to allow community members to participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present via Zoom videoconference were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson, all connecting remotely from locations in Troy, Michigan. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Cross, Haezebrouck, Conaton, Harris and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 12 additional members of the audience. The minutes were submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION - TSD Mission Moment. Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction Christine DiPilato, Natalie Haezebrouck, Director of Teaching & Learning, and Evan Rokicki, Curriculum & Instruction Specialist for Social Studies, introduced Zach MacIntosh, eighth grade teacher at Baker Middle School, who was named the 2020 Michigan History Teacher of the Year. The award is presented annually by the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History, described as the nation's leading organization dedicated to American history education; each year the institute selects one exceptional K-12 American history teacher from finalists in each state. In 2012 Zach received his bachelor's degree from Oakland University and began teaching history in the fall of 2012. In 2015 he received his Master's Degree from Saginaw Valley State University and followed up with an Education Specialist Degree in 2019 from Arkansas State University. His passion for history and technology have been combined in his classroom with an eye toward making history relevant to the younger generation, and he has built lasting relationships with students in the Troy School District around history as they critically analyze the American past. Zach was congratulated by all Board members and District administrators.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION. Dr. Beth Feiten, Director of the School and Field Services Office (Student Teaching Office) of Oakland University, thanked the District administration, teachers and staff for their support and partnership during the pandemic.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA (Resolution 20-089). It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the November 10, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 17, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for October 2020; and Budget Adjustment #1. He recommended that the current plan be reconfirmed by the Board.

Reconfirmation of COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan (Resolution 20-092). The minutes recite that Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support all schools in Michigan as they plan for a return of Pre-K through Post High School education in the fall, and that under this order Michigan school districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan laying out how they will cope with the disease across the various phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan. Each district must submit a reconfirmation plan to its Board of Education for approval on a monthly basis, and once approved must post its Preparedness Plan on the district's website home page for public access. It was moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Troy Board of Education approve the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan. On roll call vote, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond No, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes. Yes: 6 (Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hauff, Philippart), No: 1 (Hammond).

Dr. Machesky again welcomed Mr. Cornelius Godfrey to the District, thanked the unsung heroes who have helped support the District during the pandemic, and shared the passing of Pete Maurer, retired Baker Middle School teacher, extending condolences to Pete's family. Mr. Schmidt wished everyone happy holidays and shared his gratitude for everyone and for the students.

Mr. Schmidt asked the Board if anyone had questions. ADJOURNMENT. The meeting was adjourned at 8:10 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Twenty-slide Troy School District presentation titled "2026 TSD Blueprint – World Class for All," presented September 21, 2021, organizing the district's strategic plan around four color-coded pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning), and Gold (Building Capacity). The stated mission is "Ensuring learning for all," centering the ONETROY community, with each pillar carrying an overview, objectives and key results. Named targets include applying for 16-32 additional GSRP slots from the State of Michigan in 2021-22 and opening an additional 2-3 PreK classrooms serving 40-60 students.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Format**
Twenty-slide PowerPoint, "2026 TSD Blueprint – World Class for All" (Project 2026 Blueprint), on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for September 21, 2021. Slides 1-3 cover title, Introduction, and Key Themes and Next Steps; slide 19 is a Summary.

**Mission and Vision (Re)Fresh – slide 4**
Troy School District mission: "Ensuring learning for all. Centers ONETROY community." Four framing statements: Early Childhood to Career – expands on research with access through career; Equity and Well-Being – ensures safety, belonging, and connection; Deep Learning – ensures learning for all throughout the system; Building Capacity – expands to include students, staff, and community as learners.

**Core values and accountability – slides 5-6**
World Class for All pillars are described as carefully aligned to core values of Collaboration, Deep Learning, and Focus. The accountability plan holds the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results.

**Green Pillar – Early Childhood to Career (slides 7-9)**
Objectives: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds and access for all; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students through high-quality career and technical education that expands access to computer science, connects underrepresented students to in-demand careers in high-growth sectors, and builds partnerships with higher education institutions and employers for work-based learning, credentials and college credit.
Key results: apply for 16-32 additional GSRP slots from the State of Michigan in the 2021-22 school year; open an additional 2-3 PreK classrooms (40-60 students) in 2021-22; schedule two meetings and/or site visits with local legislators regarding free preschool for all; building leaders participate in Career Readiness meetings and report back to administrative and building teams twice during 2021-22; the Green Pillar Team researches the Portrait of a Graduate framework during two Career Readiness meetings and develops a Portrait of a Graduate survey by the close of the 2021-22 school year.

**Red Pillar – Equity and Well-Being (slides 10-12)**
Overview: safely reopen schools and support students, particularly those disproportionately impacted by the pandemic; fund additional investments supporting the whole child, including community schools providing wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities in all school communities.
Key results: increase social work and counseling support in all buildings; review and monitor student data; emphasize adult learning in well-being and equity; create a common understanding of a system of support at all levels.

**Blue Pillar – Deep Learning (slides 13-15)**
Objectives: create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice; improve technology access for students and families with quality training; pursue global best practices in all content areas; assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities.
Key results: monitor instructional data at least 3 times per year; expand job-embedded coaching; leverage technology for all students in all buildings.

**Gold Pillar – Building Capacity (slides 16-18)**
Objectives: improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, and support current educators; continue job-embedded professional learning for all staff; provide professional learning for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.
Key results: expand hiring networks; expand job-embedded coaching; implement a Delayed Start Model of 90 minutes to ensure collaboration through professional learning, with emphasis on advancing strategic planning priorities; ensure all staff are trained in all departments.

CORE VALUES AND ACCOUNTABILITY PLAN. **Item and Source**
Agenda item 8.B., meeting of October 19, 2021. "Troy School District — Report to the Board of Education, June 30, 2021," prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC. Report letters are dated October 5, 2021. Signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Manager). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office. Contents: Results of the Audit, pages 1-4; Informational Items, pages 5-15.

**Required Auditor Communications**
The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; the audit followed the scope and timing set at the planning meeting of August 13, 2021, under U.S. GAAS and Government Auditing Standards, with a separate internal control and compliance letter and a 2 CFR Part 200 single audit report both dated October 5, 2021. No new accounting policies were adopted and none changed during 2021. There were no transactions lacking authoritative guidance, no significant difficulties or disagreements with management, and no consultations with other independent accountants. Management corrected all immaterial misstatements and signed a representation letter dated October 5, 2021.

**Most Sensitive Estimates**
The District's share of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB Statements Nos. 68 and 75, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services:

| Estimate at June 30, 2021 | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Net pension liability | $308,094,061 |
| Net OPEB liability | $48,088,931 |

**State Aid Background**
The May 2020 Revenue Estimating Conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil; the August 2020 conference produced an actual proration of $175 per pupil for 2019-2020. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at 2019-2020 levels with a $65 one-time per pupil payment. The 2020-2021 target foundation allowance was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111. A one-year "super blend" pupil count weighted the 2019-2020 count at 75 percent and the 2020-2021 count at 25 percent. For 2021-2022 all districts move to a target foundation of $8,700 per pupil with at least a $171 per pupil increase; for hold harmless districts such as Troy, that $171 arrives as $115 of foundation allowance and $56 of Section 20m funding. Pupil counts return to 90 percent fall / 10 percent spring weighting.

**MPSERS and Federal Funding**
The estimated 2020-2021 MPSERS contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent of payroll, and from 20.96 to 28.21 percent net of state support. District receipts were $1,070,809 in Section 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 in 147e. For 2022 the overall rate is expected to rise to 43 percent from 42 percent, with net cost approximating 28 percent. Coronavirus Relief Fund distributions of approximately $362 per pupil totaled $4,588,959 for the District and were fully expended in the year ended June 30, 2021. ESSER I was awarded at $246,411, with ESSER II and III estimated at $843,258 and $1,893,840. Against the $450 per pupil ESSER II floor, the District qualified for a state equalization payment of $5,036,199 received across the May through August 2021 state aid payments, recognized partly in fiscal 2021 with the remainder in fiscal 2022. A $1,093 per student floor was set for ESSER III, though its legality was being questioned federally.

**Fund Balance**
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000 in 2020-2021, raising General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent, about 10.3 weeks of operation; the statewide average at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent, roughly 8 weeks.

**Upcoming Standards and Advisory Topics**
GASB Statement No. 87 (Leases) and SAS No. 134, issued May 2019, both take effect for June 30, 2022. Agenda item 8.B. for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of October 19, 2021 is the annual "Report to the Board of Education" for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021, prepared by the District's independent auditors, Plante & Moran, PLLC. The transmittal letter and all component letters are dated October 5, 2021. The report is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Manager. The firm records its thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities. The document is organized in two parts: Results of the Audit at pages 1-4 and Informational Items at pages 5-15.

RESULTS OF THE AUDIT. Plante & Moran audited the financial statements of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2021 and issued its report thereon dated October 5, 2021. The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, with a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 covering internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing. Scope and timing followed the planning meeting of August 13, 2021.

Significant audit findings: significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2021. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance or consensus, and none were recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2021 were $308,094,061 for the pension plan and $48,088,931 for the OPEB plan, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear. There were no significant difficulties with management, no disagreements, and no consultations with other independent accountants; management corrected all immaterial misstatements and signed a representation letter dated October 5, 2021. A 2 CFR Part 200 audit of federal programs was completed, with the compliance report dated October 5, 2021. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and noted nothing materially inconsistent.

STATE AID FUNDING BACKGROUND. Spring 2020 predictions of negative impacts to the School Aid Fund led to two Revenue Estimating Conferences, the scheduled one in May 2020 and an additional conference in August 2020. The May conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil, and many districts adopted a final 2020 budget amendment reflecting it; by August 2020 the result was a proration of $175 per pupil for the 2019-2020 fiscal year. Federal assistance began in March 2020 and arrived in waves through 2020 and 2021. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at the 2019-2020 level, no prorations were required, and a $65 one-time per pupil payment was provided; the State also funded districts that fell below a minimum per pupil threshold from the new Educational Stabilization Fund federal program. For 2021-2022, all schools reach the target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap between base and target foundations, with all schools including hold harmless districts receiving at least a $171 per pupil increase, plus progress on School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations covering special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and Great Start Readiness (GSRP).

2021 FUNDING IMPLICATIONS FOR THE DISTRICT. The 2020-2021 target foundation allowance (formerly the basic foundation allowance) was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111; the District received a one-time per pupil payment of $65 that was not added to the foundation formula and not retained for 2021-2022. A one-year "super blend" pupil count combined the 2019-2020 count weighted at 75 percent with the 2020-2021 count weighted at 25 percent.

MPSERS COST SUPPORT. Contributions are computed as a percentage of payroll and the required rate continues to increase. The estimated contribution rate for 2020-2021 ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, with the rate net of state funding support, paid directly by the employer, ranging from 20.96 to 28.21 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act. The District received $1,070,809 in 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 of 147e. The total cost of retirement contributions in 2020-2021 represents approximately 42 percent of covered payroll recognized as expenditure, with the District responsible for approximately a 28 percent contribution net of state support.

CORONAVIRUS RELIEF FUND. In summer 2020, approximately $362 per pupil was provided to districts by the Michigan Department of Education through summer state aid payments; the total available to Troy School District was $4,588,959. Because the funding was not approved until July 2020, revenue recognition was deferred to fiscal year 2021, and for the year ended June 30, 2021 the District fully expended the award and recognized the related federal revenue.

PANDEMIC-RELATED FEDERAL FUNDING AND ESSER. Key sources are the Education Stabilization Fund (ESF), whose principal programs are the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) Fund and the Governor's Education Emergency Relief (GEER) Fund, and the Coronavirus Relief Fund. Reimbursement claims could reach back to March 2020. ESSER grants come in three waves: ESSER I, ESSER II (phases 1 and 2), and ESSER III. The District's ESSER I award was $246,411, with ESSER II and ESSER III estimates of $843,258 and $1,893,840. Many districts did not receive phase 1 ESSER II award letters by June 30, 2021, deferring that revenue to fiscal 2022; phase 2 of ESSER II and ESSER III awards become available in fiscal year 2022. ESSER allocations follow the Title I model using economically disadvantaged demographics, so the Legislature and governor set a per pupil floor of $450 for ESSER II; based on its ESSER II level, the District qualified for an equalization payment of $5,036,199 received over the May through August 2021 state aid payments, recognized partly as fiscal 2021 revenue with the remainder in fiscal 2022.

2022 FUNDING IMPLICATIONS. The May 2021 Revenue Estimating Conference was optimistic for 2022, 2023, and 2024. Districts not at the target level in 2021 move to the new $8,700 per pupil target; those already at or above the former $8,529 target receive the $171 per pupil increase. For hold harmless districts such as Troy, the $171 increase is expected in two pieces: $115 per pupil of foundation allowance and $56 per pupil of Section 20m funding. The State set an ESSER III funding floor of $1,093 per student, but the federal government has begun questioning its legality. Pupil membership returns to the pre-fiscal year 2021 method for 2021-2022, weighted 90 percent fall and 10 percent spring. Resources went to summer 2021 programming, credit recovery, and before- and after-school programming through ESSER II plus state appropriations. For 2021-2022 the overall MPSERS contribution rate is expected to increase to 43 percent from 42 percent, with net cost to the District approximating 28 percent.

LOOKING FORWARD TO 2023 AND BEYOND. 2021 carries a projected surplus into 2022, with surpluses expected for 2023 and 2024. Monitoring factors include the economic "bounce back," tapering federal stimulus, the return to in-class instruction, learning loss, enrollment changes, personnel shortages, staffing costs, and retirement system cost trends. The next Revenue Estimating Conference will occur in January 2022.

GRANTS MANAGEMENT AND BUDGETING. The report catalogs increased grants management burden across leadership, board members, the business office, staff, procurement, information technology, support services, and facilities, and recommends a fiscal 2022 risk assessment of key processes and controls. Budget guidance covers multiyear revenue forecasting, monitoring pupil counts, separating recurring contractual payroll from variable pandemic-funded payroll, and budgeting one-time uses of assistance. Federal grant program end dates are laddered through 2024.

MPSERS PLAN STATUS. The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2020 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $35 billion, an increase from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, an increase of approximately 3.5 percent, driven largely by less than favorable actuarial experience. At September 30, 2020 the retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $5.4 billion, a decrease from $7.3 billion at September 30, 2019, a decrease of approximately 26 percent, reflecting a reduction in the health care cost trend rate from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable plan experience from lower than projected health benefit costs.

FUND BALANCE. During the 2020-2021 school year the District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, roughly equal to average operating costs for an 8-week period. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent, equal to approximately 10.3 weeks of operation. The report cautions that Consumer Price Index growth and decisions on spending COVID-19 relief funds will pressure fund balance in 2021-2022.

CYBERSECURITY AND IT. Education remains a top ransomware target. The "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act," introduced in the House in June 2021, would appropriate $10 million yearly for two years for a school cybersecurity program. The auditors note weak passwords such as "August2021," raise questions about PII and FERPA-covered data on file-sharing sites, flash drives, and personal email, and offer an external vulnerability assessment plus a broader IT assessment covering governance, IT staffing, external service providers, service delivery, network and device management, and cybersecurity policies.

ACCOUNTING AND AUDITING CHANGES. GASB Statement No. 87 (Leases) is effective for the District's June 30, 2022 financial statements, requiring lessees to recognize a lease liability and intangible right-of-use asset and lessors a lease receivable and deferred inflow of resources, with an inventory of lease and embedded-lease contracts needed. SAS No. 134, "Auditor Reporting and Amendments, including Amendments Addressing Disclosures in the Audit of Financial Statements," issued by the AICPA Auditing Standards Board in May 2019, takes effect for the June 30, 2022 audited financial statements, moving the opinion to the top of the letter, expanding the basis of opinion section, explaining materiality and reasonable assurance, enhancing going concern reporting, and introducing key audit matters. The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013; an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" was issued in June 2020 with a comment period ending February 2021 on which Plante & Moran commented, and the GASB goal is final standards by June 2022. Proposed changes include more MD&A information, a budget-to-actual column showing variances between original and amended budget, renaming "revenue" as "inflows of resources" and "expenditures" as "outflows of resources," and replacing modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" covering amounts converted to or paid in cash within 12 months of year end, versus today's 60-day receivable rule. Phased adoption would apply at June 30, 2025 for districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under $75 million. A related GASB preliminary views document, "Revenue and Expense Recognition," was released in June 2020, with a standard anticipated during 2025.
